item.title: Cloudflare Tunnel vs Access: Do You Need Both?
item.category: "Network Security" , "Self-Hosted" , "Cloud Security"
item.description: Understand Cloudflare Tunnel vs Access, choose protection for a home dashboard, and avoid publishing a private application without authentication.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Cloudflare Tunnel</strong> connects your application to Cloudflare. <strong>Cloudflare Access</strong> controls who reaches it. For a private home dashboard exposed through a public hostname, use both. A functioning tunnel alone does not add an identity check. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare’s application publishing guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cloudflare’s application publishing guide</a> </span> explains this distinction.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain the route:</strong> distinguish the connector, origin, and identity check.</li> <li><strong>Configure a policy:</strong> admit named people to one private dashboard.</li> <li><strong>Evaluate protection:</strong> test allowed, denied, and alternate access paths.</li> <li><strong>Design access:</strong> document separate requirements for visitors and automation.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Audience:</strong> home-server owners deciding how to protect a browser dashboard. The worked example assumes an active domain on Cloudflare, a working local web application, and permission to administer both. <strong>Estimated effort:</strong> 20–30 minutes for the policy exercise after connector setup. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> beginner to intermediate.</p> <p><strong>Reading path:</strong> start with the product roles, follow one request, then configure and review a small policy. Finish by writing an access specification for your own service.</p> <h2 id="what-each-product-does"> <a href="#what-each-product-does" title="What Each Product Does">What Each Product Does</a> <a href="#what-each-product-does" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Each Product Does">#</a> </h2> <p>The <strong>origin</strong> is the server running your application. The <strong><code>cloudflared</code></strong> connector initiates connections from your infrastructure to Cloudflare, so the origin does not need a publicly routable IP address. Requests and responses then travel over the established connection. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare Tunnel overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cloudflare Tunnel overview</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Question</th> <th>Tunnel</th> <th>Access</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>How does Cloudflare reach my server?</strong></td> <td>Establishes the connection</td> <td>Does not replace origin connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Who gets through?</strong></td> <td>Does not supply a user login by itself</td> <td>Evaluates configured access policies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What do I configure?</strong></td> <td>Connector and application route</td> <td>Application, identity provider, and policies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>What does success prove?</strong></td> <td>The origin is reachable through the route</td> <td>A request satisfied the configured policy</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>An <strong>identity provider (IdP)</strong> authenticates the visitor. An <strong>Access policy</strong> defines an action and matching criteria. Allow admits matching users. Bypass disables Access enforcement for matching traffic. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Access policy reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Access policy reference</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="follow-one-browser-request"> <a href="#follow-one-browser-request" title="Follow One Browser Request">Follow One Browser Request</a> <a href="#follow-one-browser-request" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Follow One Browser Request">#</a> </h2> <p>For <strong><code>dashboard.example.com</code></strong>, the logical request path is:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Browser -> Cloudflare Access -> tunnel connection -> cloudflared -> dashboard </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> | </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> +-> identity provider when authentication is needed </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The <strong>connector initiates the tunnel connection outward</strong> from your network. Browser requests then travel toward the origin over this established connection. An outbound connection carrying inbound application requests is the central reason Tunnel works without a conventional forwarded origin port. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tunnel connection model"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tunnel connection model</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Application permissions</strong> remain another decision. Admission to a dashboard does not automatically specify who should edit its settings or delete its data. If the application has viewer and administrator roles, configure and test those roles separately.</p> <p>For example, <strong>a family viewer</strong> needs permission to see backup status, while you need permission to change backup destinations. Write those requirements before selecting identities. Two people passing the same Access check should not automatically receive the same application privileges.</p> <h2 id="when-you-need-both"> <a href="#when-you-need-both" title="When You Need Both">When You Need Both</a> <a href="#when-you-need-both" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="When You Need Both">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>The audience determines the protection.</strong> Compare these arrangements before publishing a route:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Intended audience</th> <th>Suggested arrangement</th> <th>Review before use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Anyone reading a public website</strong></td> <td>Tunnel if needed for origin connectivity</td> <td>Public exposure is intentional</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>You and a few family members</strong></td> <td>Tunnel plus Access</td> <td>Allow only the intended identities</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>An existing public origin</strong></td> <td>Access with separate origin protection</td> <td>Direct origin access must not bypass the check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A scheduled script</strong></td> <td>Tunnel plus a Service Auth policy</td> <td>The client supports the authentication method</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Access without Tunnel</strong> is supported for an already reachable origin. Protect alternate routes to the server as well. Cloudflare recommends creating the Access application first when publishing a new tunnel route. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Self-hosted application requirements"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Self-hosted application requirements</a> </span> .</p> <p><em>For a private home dashboard reached through a public hostname, start with Tunnel plus Access.</em></p> <h2 id="configure-a-dashboard-policy"> <a href="#configure-a-dashboard-policy" title="Configure a Dashboard Policy">Configure a Dashboard Policy</a> <a href="#configure-a-dashboard-policy" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Configure a Dashboard Policy">#</a> </h2> <p>Use this <strong>worked configuration</strong> for two intended visitors. Replace both example addresses with identities you control. Create the Access application before adding the public tunnel route.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Application:</strong> open Zero Trust → Access controls → Applications and create a self-hosted application with a public hostname.</li> <li><strong>Hostname:</strong> enter the dedicated dashboard hostname. Leave the path unrestricted for this whole-hostname example.</li> <li><strong>Policy:</strong> create an Allow policy named <code>Dashboard viewers</code>.</li> <li><strong>Identity selector:</strong> add an Include rule using Emails, with <code>alice@example.com</code> and <code>bob@example.com</code> replaced by your two intended addresses.</li> <li><strong>Login:</strong> select the identity provider used by those visitors and choose a deliberate session duration.</li> <li><strong>Route:</strong> save the application, then connect the hostname to the dashboard through your tunnel.</li> </ol> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official application workflow"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official application workflow</a> </span> documents these settings. <strong>Expected result:</strong> a new visitor encounters authentication before reaching the application. Complete the denied-identity test below before relying on the policy.</p> <h2 id="interpret-the-rule-logic"> <a href="#interpret-the-rule-logic" title="Interpret the Rule Logic">Interpret the Rule Logic</a> <a href="#interpret-the-rule-logic" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interpret the Rule Logic">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Include</strong> combines alternatives with OR. <strong>Require</strong> adds mandatory conditions with AND. <strong>Exclude</strong> removes matching users. Adding another Include condition broadens the eligible group. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Access rule semantics"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/policies/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Access rule semantics</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Policy fragment</th> <th>Logical effect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Include Alice or Bob</strong></td> <td>Either named identity qualifies</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Include Alice, Include a country</strong></td> <td>People matching the country also qualify</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Include Alice, Require a country</strong></td> <td>Alice must also match the country</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Policy-review exercise:</strong> your requirement names only Alice and Bob, but your colleague adds a country as another Include condition. Reject the change because it admits an additional population. Geography does not establish membership in your household.</p> <h2 id="authenticate-scheduled-scripts"> <a href="#authenticate-scheduled-scripts" title="Authenticate Scheduled Scripts">Authenticate Scheduled Scripts</a> <a href="#authenticate-scheduled-scripts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Authenticate Scheduled Scripts">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>service token</strong> contains a Client ID and Client Secret for automated requests. Configure the application policy to accept the token using <strong>Service Auth</strong>. Creating a token without the corresponding policy does not grant application access. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare service tokens"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/service-credentials/service-tokens/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/service-credentials/service-tokens/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cloudflare service tokens</a> </span> .</p> <p>For a backup script or monitoring check, keep the <strong>secret</strong> in the tool’s protected credential storage. Give each integration a distinct token name and a deliberate expiration date. Rotate or revoke its token when retiring the integration. The service-token documentation covers these lifecycle operations.</p> <p><strong>Client compatibility</strong> deserves an explicit check. A tool expecting an API response will not necessarily handle an interactive browser login. Confirm its support for request headers or another supported authentication method before choosing the policy.</p> <h2 id="test-access-decisions"> <a href="#test-access-decisions" title="Test Access Decisions">Test Access Decisions</a> <a href="#test-access-decisions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test Access Decisions">#</a> </h2> <p>Treat these as <strong>acceptance checks</strong> for your deployment:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Check</th> <th>Evidence to record</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Signed-out visitor</strong></td> <td>Access intercepts a request from a fresh browser session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Allowed identity</strong></td> <td>The intended application loads after sign-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disallowed identity</strong></td> <td>An unlisted account receives no application access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Alternate route</strong></td> <td>Old DNS names and origin ports provide no unintended access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Automation</strong></td> <td>The approved client succeeds and a request without its credential fails</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A visible login screen</strong> proves only one path encountered authentication. Test the denied case and alternate routes too. These are suggested checks, not results from a deployed example.</p> <h2 id="check-the-origin-boundary"> <a href="#check-the-origin-boundary" title="Check the Origin Boundary">Check the Origin Boundary</a> <a href="#check-the-origin-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check the Origin Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An origin trusting Access identity</strong> should validate the signed application token. Cloudflare forwards it in the <strong><code>Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion</code></strong> header. A header’s presence alone does not prove authenticity. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare JWT validation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/validating-json/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/authorization-cookie/validating-json/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Cloudflare JWT validation</a> </span> .</p> <p>A <strong>JSON Web Token (JWT)</strong> carries signed claims. Use the documented validation approach, including the expected issuer and application audience, when integrating Access identity into an origin. Decoding a token and reading an email field is insufficient validation.</p> <p><strong>Issuer</strong> identifies the authority issuing the token. <strong>Audience</strong> identifies its intended application. Check token validity and expiration through a supported validation library, instead of implementing signature checks from scratch.</p> <p><strong>Keep the boundary explicit:</strong> identify where validation happens and which routes reach the application. An old port forward or alternate hostname deserves its own review, even after the main hostname passes every browser test.</p> <h2 id="troubleshoot-policy-mismatches"> <a href="#troubleshoot-policy-mismatches" title="Troubleshoot Policy Mismatches">Troubleshoot Policy Mismatches</a> <a href="#troubleshoot-policy-mismatches" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshoot Policy Mismatches">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>Next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>An unexpected visitor gets through</strong></td> <td>Review Include conditions, Bypass policies, and hostname coverage</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>An intended visitor is denied</strong></td> <td>Compare the signed-in identity with the exact selector values</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A script receives a login page</strong></td> <td>Review its credential and Service Auth policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>An admitted viewer edits settings</strong></td> <td>Review the application’s own role assignments</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Session behavior</strong> also affects retesting. Access has several session durations, including application and global sessions. Record the session setting and use a fresh session when checking a new identity. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Access session management"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/access-settings/session-management/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/access-settings/session-management/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Access session management</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="write-your-access-specification"> <a href="#write-your-access-specification" title="Write Your Access Specification">Write Your Access Specification</a> <a href="#write-your-access-specification" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Write Your Access Specification">#</a> </h2> <p>Create a <strong>short specification</strong> before adding another service:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Service and hostname: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Human identities allowed: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application roles required: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Automation credential and expiry: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Other routes to the origin: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Where Access tokens are validated: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Allowed-identity test result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Denied-identity test result: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Completion criterion:</strong> another administrator should understand who gets access, how each client authenticates, and which evidence proves denial. If you add a monitoring integration later, update its credential entry and repeat the unauthenticated request check.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Follow the site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare Tunnel setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-setup-and-use-cloudflare-tunnels/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-setup-and-use-cloudflare-tunnels/" rel="follow me" >Cloudflare Tunnel setup guide</a> </span> for connector setup, then apply the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official Access application workflow"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/access-controls/applications/http-apps/self-hosted-public-app/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official Access application workflow</a> </span> . For a cellular connection, read <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="T-Mobile Home Internet port-forwarding limits"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/t-mobile-home-internet-port-forwarding/"> <a href="/articles/t-mobile-home-internet-port-forwarding/" rel="follow me" >T-Mobile Home Internet port-forwarding limits</a> </span> before choosing your remote-access route.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Flock Safety's Sales Pitch: Warrantless Access to Every Movement
item.category: "Privacy Technology" , "Digital Rights" , "Surveillance" , "Legal Analysis" , "Counter Surveillance"
item.description: Flock Safety does not sell cameras. It sells a subscription to warrantless movement data. Here is how the sales pitch works, how it runs against the Fourth Amendment, and why the fight is about the pitch, not the company.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Flock Safety does not sell cameras.</strong> The company sells a searchable record of where vehicles and people go, delivered to law enforcement as a subscription with no warrant and no delay. Watch the sales pitch instead of the hardware, because the pitch is the constitutional problem.</p> <p><em>The video below traces the argument end to end. It names the product, quotes the Fourth Amendment, walks the relevant court cases, and shows the two contradictory pitches Flock makes to different audiences.</em></p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { yieldToMain(function () { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); }, "user-visible"); }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style> <p>The source video, <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?</a> </span> from the T-Rex Lab channel, lays out the full case. The write-up below keeps the claims and adds the supporting law.</p> <!--more--> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>The camera is a decoy.</strong> The product is the database, and the camera only feeds it.</li> <li><strong>The Fourth Amendment reaches movement records.</strong> Jones and Carpenter extend protection to continuous location tracking.</li> <li><strong>Flock sells access, not data.</strong> The wording reclassifies a search as a query and a record as an access plan.</li> <li><strong>The pitch changes by audience.</strong> Law enforcement hears “no warrants.” The public hears “small and cautious.”</li> <li><strong>Watch the pitch, not the company.</strong> Every competitor selling warrantless access to private movement is the same fight.</li> </ul> <hr> <h2 id="what-the-company-sells"> <a href="#what-the-company-sells" title="What the Company Sells">What the Company Sells</a> <a href="#what-the-company-sells" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Company Sells">#</a> </h2> <p>Flock enters a market where cameras are already everywhere. Tens of millions of commercial cameras watch storefronts. Doorbell cameras sit on nearly half of American homes. Officers wear body cameras and drive dash cameras, and every phone carries several cameras.</p> <p><strong>Cameras are not scarce, so Flock does not sell cameras.</strong> Access to crime footage is not scarce either: victims hand their recordings straight to departments, and phone video of a crime often lands on social media before an officer asks for it. <strong>Automated license plate readers are not new</strong> either. The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on the traffic signals maintained by transportation departments.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Flock does not sell</th> <th>Why</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Cameras</strong></td> <td>Commercial, doorbell, body, dash, and phone cameras already cover most public space</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Access to footage</strong></td> <td>Victims and bystanders supply footage directly, and phone video spreads online</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>License plate readers</strong></td> <td>The technology dates to the 1970s and already runs on traffic signals</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>The scarce thing is the database.</strong> Flock aggregates plate reads, locations, and timestamps into a searchable record of movement, then sells access to it. The pitch to departments comes down to one line worth remembering: the same information a warrant would produce, but with no warrant and no wait.</p> <hr> <h2 id="a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction"> <a href="#a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction" title="A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction">A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction</a> <a href="#a-warrant-is-supposed-to-add-friction" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Warrant Is Supposed to Add Friction">#</a> </h2> <p>Phone carriers, car makers, and phone vendors each hold large location stores. Those stores carry legal friction. A request for one person’s movement history needs a warrant, and a warrant needs probable cause, a judge, and a written record. Courts have repeatedly narrowed the broad geo-fence warrants after challenges.</p> <p>Flock sells an equivalent record without the friction. Its stated position is simple: movement on public roads is public, so no warrant applies.</p> <p>The asymmetry is the whole business. The same movement data costs a warrant when a carrier holds it and nothing when Flock holds it. Removing the warrant removes the record of the search, and the record of the search is the part the public audits.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-fourth-amendment"> <a href="#the-fourth-amendment" title="The Fourth Amendment">The Fourth Amendment</a> <a href="#the-fourth-amendment" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Fourth Amendment">#</a> </h2> <p>The amendment reads as a defense against general searches. Its full text:</p> <blockquote> <p>The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.</p> </blockquote> <p>The amendment responds to the general warrants, called writs of assistance, in use before independence. Those writs named no specific place or person and carried no expiry. Officials searched anywhere, at any time, on vague suspicion. The amendment rejects the practice by tying every search to probable cause, a sworn statement, and a particular description.</p> <p>Flock’s service removes all three in one step: no probable cause, no oath, no particular description. The video’s point is blunt. A subscription dispensing with the warrant dispenses with the entire safeguard.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-case-law"> <a href="#the-case-law" title="The Case Law">The Case Law</a> <a href="#the-case-law" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Case Law">#</a> </h2> <p>Two lines of authority collide here.</p> <p>The older line holds recording what happens on a public road needs no warrant, because a person on a public road keeps no reasonable expectation of privacy in the movements seen there. Flock leans on this line and the 1984 case the video discusses.</p> <p>The newer line pulls the other way. <strong>United States v. Jones</strong> (2012) held a GPS tracker fixed to a vehicle, and followed for weeks, is a search needing a warrant even on public roads. <strong>Carpenter v. United States</strong> (2018) reached the same result for cell-site location records held by wireless carriers, because a person keeps a reasonable expectation of privacy in the record of their physical movements.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Case</th> <th>Year</th> <th>Result</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Public-recording line</strong></td> <td>1984</td> <td>Recording movement from a public corner needs no warrant, since an officer present sees the same thing</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>United States v. Jones</strong></td> <td>2012</td> <td>A GPS device tracking a car over a sustained period needs a warrant, even on public roads</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Carpenter v. United States</strong></td> <td>2018</td> <td>Cell-site location records need a warrant, since a person keeps privacy in the record of their movements</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Chhatri v. United States</strong></td> <td>cited in the video</td> <td>Location shared with a third party stays protected, so the warrant requirement survives</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Flock’s product is the comprehensive movement record Jones and Carpenter protect. The company argues its cameras escape those rulings because a sensor, not a GPS unit or a cell tower, gathers the positions. The distinction is in the sensor, not in the underlying record.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="the-loophole-in-their-own-words"> <a href="#the-loophole-in-their-own-words" title="The Loophole in Their Own Words">The Loophole in Their Own Words</a> <a href="#the-loophole-in-their-own-words" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Loophole in Their Own Words">#</a> </h2> <p>A series of word choices does the legal work. Each one rewrites the same product out of the reach of the cases above.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Sells access, not the record.</strong> Flock states it sells a subscription to query the database, so it sells no comprehensive record of movement.</li> <li><strong>Shares derived data, not your data.</strong> The wording restyles every plate read, timestamp, and route as mined material, so no raw personal data changes hands.</li> <li><strong>Queried, not searched.</strong> The Fourth Amendment stops unreasonable searches, and Flock frames every lookup as a query, so no search occurs.</li> </ul> <p><em>Each phrase relabels the same act. The activity stays identical to the thing a warrant would guard. Only the noun changes.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="two-contradictory-pitches"> <a href="#two-contradictory-pitches" title="Two Contradictory Pitches">Two Contradictory Pitches</a> <a href="#two-contradictory-pitches" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Two Contradictory Pitches">#</a> </h2> <p>Flock sells the same service two ways at once, and the versions contradict each other.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Audience</th> <th>The pitch</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Law enforcement</strong></td> <td>Wide, deep, and fast search, no delays, no warrants</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>The public and commissioners</strong></td> <td>Small, limited, safe, slow, and cautious, tied to lower crime</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The statements conflict. A database searched wide, deep, and fast with no warrants is not small or cautious in any sense the public hears. The one clause both sides share is a promise of lower crime, and the promise carries the sale. Many commissioners voting for cameras hold this belief honestly and never see the tool as mass surveillance.</p> <hr> <h2 id="what-the-records-show"> <a href="#what-the-records-show" title="What the Records Show">What the Records Show</a> <a href="#what-the-records-show" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Records Show">#</a> </h2> <p>Concrete examples sharpen the concern beyond prediction.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Pflugerville, Texas.</strong> A town of roughly 70,000 people mounted 28 cameras after a promise of local control over its data. In six months the local department filed about 5,000 queries, and a public records request surfaced 1.66 million outside queries from 469 other agencies. The town now uninstalls the cameras.</li> <li><strong>Knox County, Tennessee.</strong> A 140-camera contract ended this week by unanimous commissioner vote. A deputy signed the $274,000 deal through installment orders of $24,990 each, ten dollars below the threshold requiring a commission vote. The deputy and ten colleagues face an indictment over roughly $300,000 in spending the video notes is separate from the camera system.</li> <li><strong>Chicago, Illinois.</strong> Years earlier a council member faced charges over a $130 million red-light camera deal with Redflex. The contract ended, yet the cameras stayed mounted and restarted under a new vendor without a missed day of service.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Demos run on live data.</strong> The video reports Flock sales teams demonstrated the platform using real private records, not simulated ones. Their example searches read as a profiling tool: a vehicle with a political sticker, a truck with a Trump flag, a person wearing a mask, a person holding a weapon. A list of everyone holding a weapon in an open-carry state is not a suspect list. It is pre-crime demographic profiling.</p> <hr> <h2 id="not-about-the-camera-company"> <a href="#not-about-the-camera-company" title="Not About the Camera Company">Not About the Camera Company</a> <a href="#not-about-the-camera-company" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Not About the Camera Company">#</a> </h2> <p>Focusing on one brand misses the larger fight. The video points to Axon, which sat among Flock’s early investors, shared software and data, and integrated Flock’s feed into its evidence.com platform. Red-light camera hardware in Chicago outlived its vendor and kept running under a new name. When one company falls, the sensors and the database stay behind for the next owner.</p> <p><strong>The defining trait is the sales pitch, not the sensor.</strong> Any company selling warrantless access to a comprehensive record of private movement repeats the same offense, whether the sensor is a camera, a phone, or something not yet invented.</p> <p>The two things worth defending stay fixed: the limits on government written into the Bill of Rights, and the separation of powers keeping jurisdictions apart. Mass surveillance erodes the first, and the loophole dissolves the second. Oppose the loophole wherever its sales pitch appears.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="follow" alt="simeononsecurity" > <button class="markdown-button"> Read the Detection Arms-Race Write-Up </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <hr> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with the sales pitch, then move to the technical and protective sides.</p> <ul> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Camera Detection Arms Race: What Changed in 2026"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-camera-detection-arms-race-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Camera Detection Arms Race: What Changed in 2026</a> </span> </strong> for the technical side of the same fight.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Cameras: Public Safety Tool or Warrantless Surveillance Machine?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-cameras-public-safety-or-surveillance-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-cameras-public-safety-or-surveillance-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Cameras: Public Safety Tool or Warrantless Surveillance Machine?</a> </span> </strong> for the surveillance framing.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Safety Camera Surveillance: Privacy and Protection"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-safety-camera-surveillance-prevalence-privacy-protection-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-safety-camera-surveillance-prevalence-privacy-protection-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock Safety Camera Surveillance: Privacy and Protection</a> </span> </strong> for how the cameras spread and what protection does.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock-You Detection: Counter-Surveillance Setup Guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/" rel="follow me" >Flock-You Detection: Counter-Surveillance Setup Guide</a> </span> </strong> for building your own detector.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Source material:</strong> the argument, figures, and quotations follow <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8OuBWAmoxE8" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >What is Flock Safety ACTUALLY Selling… and To Who?</a> </span> from the T-Rex Lab channel. The Fourth Amendment text comes from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Legal Information Institute"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/fourth_amendment"> <a href="https://www.law.cornell.edu/constitution/fourth_amendment" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Legal Information Institute</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: GrapheneOS Sandboxed Google Play Explained
item.category: "Privacy" , "Mobile Security" , "Open Source"
item.description: Learn what sandboxed Google Play changes on GrapheneOS, when a separate profile helps, and how accounts, notifications, and app compatibility fit together.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Sandboxed Google Play</strong> lets you install official Google Play components on GrapheneOS as ordinary apps. They run without the system privileges Google Play normally receives on the stock OS. Installing them is optional. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS feature overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS feature overview</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Explain isolation:</strong> distinguish app permissions from online account activity.</li> <li><strong>Place dependencies:</strong> keep a dependent app and Play in the same profile.</li> <li><strong>Test behavior:</strong> check background notifications and essential workflows.</li> <li><strong>Build a plan:</strong> record your chosen profiles, accounts, and app requirements.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Audience:</strong> GrapheneOS users deciding whether to install Google Play and where to put it. <strong>Prerequisites:</strong> a supported device with an updated GrapheneOS installation and access to your essential accounts. OS installation belongs in the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/" rel="follow me" >GrapheneOS installation guide</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> 20–30 minutes for the initial app inventory and checks, plus normal daily use to assess notification reliability. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> beginner. Start with one representative app before reorganizing your phone.</p> <h2 id="what-the-sandbox-changes"> <a href="#what-the-sandbox-changes" title="What the Sandbox Changes">What the Sandbox Changes</a> <a href="#what-the-sandbox-changes" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Sandbox Changes">#</a> </h2> <p>Android’s <strong>application sandbox</strong> separates app resources using operating-system protections. An app does not receive unrestricted access to another app’s private files. The protection applies to native code as well as code running through Android’s managed runtime. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Android application sandbox documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://source.android.com/docs/security/app-sandbox"> <a href="https://source.android.com/docs/security/app-sandbox" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Android application sandbox documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p>GrapheneOS adds a <strong>compatibility layer</strong> so official Play components function within those ordinary restrictions. Apps in the same profile still have supported ways to communicate by mutual consent. Sandboxing limits privileges, but it does not prevent every intentional exchange between apps. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Sandboxed Google Play design"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features#sandboxed-google-play" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Sandboxed Google Play design</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Concern</th> <th>Practical meaning</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Private app files</strong></td> <td>Installing Play does not grant unrestricted access to other apps’ data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Permissions</strong></td> <td>Review requested access as you would for another app</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Google-backed features</strong></td> <td>An app choosing a Google service still communicates with it</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Account activity</strong></td> <td>Signing into a service remains a separate privacy decision</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Sandboxing and account privacy</strong> answer different questions. A sandbox restricts local access. It does not erase information you deliberately submit to an online service. For example, signing into a shopping app still identifies your account to its operator.</p> <h2 id="separate-three-privacy-decisions"> <a href="#separate-three-privacy-decisions" title="Separate Three Privacy Decisions">Separate Three Privacy Decisions</a> <a href="#separate-three-privacy-decisions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Separate Three Privacy Decisions">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Local access, service use, and identity</strong> are separate questions. For an app requesting contact access and account sign-in, review each request independently:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Decision</th> <th>Question to answer</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Local permission</strong></td> <td>Does this feature need my contacts, microphone, or location?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service dependency</strong></td> <td>Which feature relies on Play services?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Online identity</strong></td> <td>Which account am I associating with this activity?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A practical example:</strong> a shopping account already contains your delivery address. Moving its app into another profile does not change the address held by the retailer. Declining contact access answers a different question about data available on your phone.</p> <p><strong>Privacy objective:</strong> write the specific exposure you want to reduce. “Keep this app away from my personal contacts” is testable. “Make this account anonymous” requires decisions beyond profile placement.</p> <h2 id="owner-profile-or-separate-profile"> <a href="#owner-profile-or-separate-profile" title="Owner Profile or Separate Profile?">Owner Profile or Separate Profile?</a> <a href="#owner-profile-or-separate-profile" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Owner Profile or Separate Profile?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Owner-profile installation</strong> is a supported, straightforward choice. Google Play remains sandboxed there. A separate user or work profile helps you choose which group of apps has Play available. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS installation guidance</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Your priority</th> <th>Starting arrangement</th> <th>Tradeoff</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Simple daily use</strong></td> <td>Keep required apps and Play in Owner</td> <td>Play is available to cooperating apps in this profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Separate Google-dependent apps</strong></td> <td>Install them together in another profile</td> <td>More profile management</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Avoid Google services</strong></td> <td>Start without Play</td> <td>Check each app’s dependencies</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Profile placement</strong> matters more than installing the same component everywhere. GrapheneOS’s FAQ explains how Play availability is scoped to selected profiles, while many apps work without it or need it for only part of their functionality. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Google services FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#google-services"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#google-services" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Google services FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><em>Use a separate profile when selective Play availability solves a specific requirement you have identified.</em></p> <h2 id="understand-profile-activity"> <a href="#understand-profile-activity" title="Understand Profile Activity">Understand Profile Activity</a> <a href="#understand-profile-activity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Understand Profile Activity">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A secondary user profile</strong> has its own app instances and data. Switching to another user and ending the previous user’s session are different actions. <strong>End session</strong> stops apps in the secondary profile and returns its encrypted storage to rest. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS encryption and profile FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#encryption"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#encryption" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS encryption and profile FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Notification forwarding</strong> optionally surfaces notifications from a user running in the background to the active user. It does not keep an ended session running. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS user-profile features"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/features"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/features" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS user-profile features</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Profile state</th> <th>Delivery condition</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Active</strong></td> <td>Test delivery inside this profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Running in background</strong></td> <td>Check forwarding to the active user</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Session ended</strong></td> <td>Apps in this profile are stopped</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>For <strong>a daily messaging app</strong>, decide whether receiving messages while using Owner is essential. A profile arrangement demanding frequent session shutdown conflicts with continuous background delivery. Make this tradeoff before moving your main conversation history.</p> <h2 id="installation-and-accounts"> <a href="#installation-and-accounts" title="Installation and Accounts">Installation and Accounts</a> <a href="#installation-and-accounts" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Installation and Accounts">#</a> </h2> <p>Open the built-in <strong>GrapheneOS App Store</strong>, select <strong>Google Play services</strong>, and install it. This also installs the dependent Play Store. Let the App Store maintain these components. Grant Play services a battery optimization exception for reliable background features such as push notifications. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Official installation instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/usage#sandboxed-google-play-installation" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Official installation instructions</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Google account sign-in</strong> is optional for functionality without an account dependency. Installing apps through the Play Store requires sign-in. Older installations also include Google Services Framework, which the project says to retain. Follow current installation instructions instead of an old three-package checklist.</p> <h2 id="test-one-app-first"> <a href="#test-one-app-first" title="Test One App First">Test One App First</a> <a href="#test-one-app-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test One App First">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a <strong>low-risk representative app</strong> to check your intended profile arrangement. Keep existing account recovery methods available throughout the exercise.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Select a profile:</strong> decide where the app belongs before installing its dependencies.</li> <li><strong>Install Play:</strong> use the official installation steps above within this profile.</li> <li><strong>Install the app:</strong> use its trusted distribution source and complete initial setup.</li> <li><strong>Review requests:</strong> approve permissions according to the feature you are testing.</li> <li><strong>Exercise one feature:</strong> send a message, open a map, or perform another reversible action.</li> <li><strong>Record the result:</strong> note the app version, OS version, profile, and exact operation.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Expected evidence:</strong> a repeatable description such as “a test message arrived with the screen locked in the active profile.” Avoid recording only “works,” which hides the feature and conditions tested.</p> <h2 id="diagnose-missing-notifications"> <a href="#diagnose-missing-notifications" title="Diagnose Missing Notifications">Diagnose Missing Notifications</a> <a href="#diagnose-missing-notifications" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Diagnose Missing Notifications">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Push notifications</strong> depend on the app’s implementation. Some apps maintain their own background connection. Others rely on Google’s Firebase Cloud Messaging. An app opening successfully does not prove its notifications work after you lock the phone. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS notification FAQ"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://grapheneos.org/faq#notifications"> <a href="https://grapheneos.org/faq#notifications" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GrapheneOS notification FAQ</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Check the delivery conditions</strong> before changing permissions across several apps:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>Narrow the investigation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messages appear only after opening</strong></td> <td>Check the app’s background delivery method and battery settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Delivery works only in its profile</strong></td> <td>Check profile activity and notification forwarding</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No delivery after End session</strong></td> <td>Start the secondary profile before testing again</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>The notification arrives silently</strong></td> <td>Inspect the app’s notification channel and sound settings</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Notification channels</strong> group an app’s notification behavior, including importance and sound. Android exposes channel controls to the user. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Android notification-channel documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/notifications/channels"> <a href="https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/notifications/channels" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Android notification-channel documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Retest one condition at a time:</strong> keep the sending device and message type fixed while changing the receiving profile’s state. Record “active,” “running in background,” or “session ended” alongside each result. This distinguishes a profile-lifecycle problem from a notification configuration problem.</p> <h2 id="evaluate-essential-workflows"> <a href="#evaluate-essential-workflows" title="Evaluate Essential Workflows">Evaluate Essential Workflows</a> <a href="#evaluate-essential-workflows" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluate Essential Workflows">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a short <strong>personal acceptance test</strong> before relying on a new setup:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Workflow</th> <th>Check on your device</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messaging</strong></td> <td>Receive a message with the screen locked</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Account access</strong></td> <td>Sign in and complete the required second factor</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Banking or payments</strong></td> <td>Test the exact function you need, including any device checks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Navigation</strong></td> <td>Obtain location with your chosen permissions</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>An app launching</strong> is only the first check. Record the app version, GrapheneOS version, and failed operation when troubleshooting. This article provides a decision framework, not a tested compatibility list.</p> <p><strong>Migration decision:</strong> keep your previous access method until each essential operation has passed. A messaging app and a banking app need different acceptance criteria. Successful message delivery says nothing about another app’s account or device checks.</p> <p>For <strong>a work login</strong>, test the complete sign-in sequence and the required second factor. For a travel app, test the feature you expect to use away from home. Choose representative actions without making unnecessary purchases or changing account security.</p> <h2 id="build-your-app-plan"> <a href="#build-your-app-plan" title="Build Your App Plan">Build Your App Plan</a> <a href="#build-your-app-plan" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build Your App Plan">#</a> </h2> <p>Complete this <strong>inventory</strong> for your five most important apps. The rows below are prompts, not compatibility claims about specific products:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>App category</th> <th>Requirement to record</th> <th>Evidence to collect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Messaging</strong></td> <td>Background delivery and profile choice</td> <td>Locked-screen and background-profile test</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Work access</strong></td> <td>Required login and second factor</td> <td>Completed sign-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Navigation</strong></td> <td>Location permission and offline needs</td> <td>A route under expected conditions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Banking</strong></td> <td>Essential supported operations</td> <td>Results for each required function</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Shopping</strong></td> <td>Account and local-data access</td> <td>Permission review and normal account use</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Write a decision</strong> for each row: chosen profile, Play dependency, account requirement, approved permissions, and fallback. Leave unknown dependencies marked unknown until you have evidence. This avoids installing additional components merely because another app needed them.</p> <p><strong>Review exercise:</strong> an app works while its secondary profile is active, then stops receiving messages after End session. The first action is to restart the profile and retest. Granting contact access would not address a stopped session.</p> <p><strong>Completion criterion:</strong> your plan should explain why each app sits in its chosen profile and which test supports relying on it. Revisit the relevant row after an update changes behavior.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GrapheneOS installation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-install-graphine-os/" rel="follow me" >GrapheneOS installation guide</a> </span> if you have not installed the OS. Then choose one profile arrangement and test your essential apps before adding extra profiles or changing broad permission settings.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Microsoft SOC Home Lab: Build Cybersecurity Experience in 2026
item.category: "Cybersecurity" , "Cloud Security" , "Career Development"
item.description: Build a Microsoft SOC home lab with Sentinel, Defender, Intune, and Entra. Practice incident investigation, validate passkey policies, and document portfolio evidence.
item.content:encoded: <p>A <strong>security operations center (SOC) home lab</strong> gives you a place to investigate alerts, explain evidence, and test defensive changes. Build a small Microsoft environment, collect its telemetry, and write up each investigation. The useful result is a repeatable investigation with supporting evidence.</p> <p>This guide develops the lab approach described in Mad Hat’s cybersecurity career video and supplied Cyber Range runbook. It uses Microsoft documentation for product requirements and separates setup, detection, and validation into measurable tasks.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Start small:</strong> one managed Windows client and one test identity support the first exercises.</li> <li><strong>Verify telemetry:</strong> a visible device or connected portal does not prove logs are arriving.</li> <li><strong>Complete the investigation:</strong> record the trigger, evidence, response, and retest.</li> <li><strong>Control spending:</strong> track licenses, retained data, networking, and compute separately.</li> <li><strong>Describe experience accurately:</strong> list the environment as a lab project on your resume.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> basic Windows administration, networking, and familiarity with virtual machines. Use a dedicated Microsoft Entra tenant and an Azure subscription reserved for the lab. Keep production identities, personal files, and employer systems outside the exercise.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> allow a weekend for the initial setup, followed by focused investigation sessions. This is a planning estimate. Trial approval, quota availability, and service provisioning affect elapsed time. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> intermediate.</p> <p>Prepare a separate administrative account and an unprivileged test user. Before testing access policies, establish and verify emergency access. Assign privileges for each setup task, then use a lower-privilege account for routine investigation.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>Lab purpose</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Sentinel</strong></td> <td>Security information and event management, or SIEM, for connected log sources</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender XDR</strong></td> <td>Correlation and investigation across licensed Microsoft security services</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender for Endpoint</strong></td> <td>Endpoint detection and response, or EDR, on onboarded devices</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Intune</strong></td> <td>Device enrollment and endpoint security policy management</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Entra ID</strong></td> <td>Identity, sign-in records, and access policy evaluation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Defender for Servers</strong></td> <td>Server protection through Defender for Cloud</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="check-licenses-first"> <a href="#check-licenses-first" title="Check Licenses First">Check Licenses First</a> <a href="#check-licenses-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Licenses First">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Microsoft 365 E5</strong> is one route to a broad lab, but access depends on the service plans and licenses assigned to the participating users. Office 365 E5 and Microsoft 365 E5 are different bundles. A single administrator’s license does not establish coverage for every test user or workload. Review the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Defender XDR prerequisites"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/prerequisites"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/prerequisites" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Defender XDR prerequisites</a> </span> before selecting a subscription.</p> <p><strong>Sentinel in the Defender portal</strong> works without E5 or Defender XDR. Adding XDR introduces its own licensing and configuration requirements. An empty incident view is not evidence of missing E5 licensing. Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Sentinel onboarding documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Sentinel onboarding documentation</a> </span> explains both configurations.</p> <p><strong>Server protection</strong> has a separate licensing path. Defender for Servers integrates with Defender for Endpoint for supported server workloads. Windows client operating systems need appropriate client coverage. Do not treat every Azure VM as an automatically licensed server. See Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Defender for Endpoint integration documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Defender for Endpoint integration documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Trial planning:</strong> confirm eligibility, expiration, renewal settings, and included services in your own account. Avoid budgeting around a promised trial duration or a fixed monthly total from a video.</p> <h2 id="set-a-spending-plan"> <a href="#set-a-spending-plan" title="Set a Spending Plan">Set a Spending Plan</a> <a href="#set-a-spending-plan" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Set a Spending Plan">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Azure budgets</strong> send notifications. They do not stop consumption when you reach a threshold. Cost reporting also has a delay. Create alerts early and review spending after each session, following Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="budget setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cost-management-billing/costs/tutorial-acm-create-budgets" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >budget setup guide</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Cost category</th> <th>Planning question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>User licenses</strong></td> <td>Which users need which service plans, and when do trials expire?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Compute</strong></td> <td>How many VM hours will each exercise require?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Storage</strong></td> <td>Which disks and snapshots remain after shutdown?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Log collection</strong></td> <td>Which tables need ingestion and how long should data remain?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Networking</strong></td> <td>Does the design include paid Bastion, public IPs, or outbound services?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Server protection</strong></td> <td>Which workloads have a paid Defender plan enabled?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Design choice:</strong> begin with one client. Add a server when an exercise needs server telemetry. Four clients and several servers add administration and cost before they add useful investigation practice.</p> <h2 id="build-the-network"> <a href="#build-the-network" title="Build the Network">Build the Network</a> <a href="#build-the-network" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build the Network">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Suggested layout:</strong> put Azure resources in a clearly named group such as <strong><code>rg-soc-lab</code></strong>. Use separate client and server subnets, explicit network security group rules, and private management access. Subnet separation alone does not block traffic between workloads.</p> <p>For a dedicated <strong>Azure Bastion</strong> deployment, follow the SKU requirements, including the reserved <strong><code>AzureBastionSubnet</code></strong> name and a <strong><code>/26</code></strong> or larger subnet for current deployments. Developer SKU uses a different deployment model. Review <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bastion configuration settings"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/configuration-settings"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/bastion/configuration-settings" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Bastion configuration settings</a> </span> before choosing a design.</p> <p>Keep RDP and SSH closed to the public internet. Restrict management traffic to the selected management path. Allow the outbound service connectivity needed for enrollment and security telemetry.</p> <p><strong>Validation:</strong> establish private management access and verify effective network rules before installing workloads. If you add a deliberately vulnerable application later, keep it inside the exercise network and restrict access to the test machines.</p> <h2 id="connect-sentinel-and-logs"> <a href="#connect-sentinel-and-logs" title="Connect Sentinel and Logs">Connect Sentinel and Logs</a> <a href="#connect-sentinel-and-logs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Connect Sentinel and Logs">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Portal setup:</strong> create a Log Analytics workspace and enable Sentinel on it. If the workspace is absent from the Defender portal, open <strong>System > Settings > Microsoft Sentinel > Connect a workspace</strong>. Verify the tenant and required Azure and Entra roles against the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="onboarding prerequisites"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-sentinel-onboard" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >onboarding prerequisites</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Log collection is a separate step.</strong> In Entra, configure diagnostic settings to send the required activity categories to the same workspace. Start with interactive sign-ins and audit events. Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Entra log integration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-integrate-activity-logs-with-azure-monitor-logs"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/howto-integrate-activity-logs-with-azure-monitor-logs" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Entra log integration guide</a> </span> covers the permissions and destination setup.</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-kusto" data-lang="kusto">SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | where UserPrincipalName =~ "soc-test@YOUR-TENANT.onmicrosoft.com" | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, ResultType, ConditionalAccessStatus, CorrelationId | order by TimeGenerated desc </code></pre><p>Run this <strong>Kusto Query Language (KQL)</strong> example in the workspace’s Logs view after generating a fresh test sign-in. Replace the sample user principal name with your lab user. The columns follow the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SigninLogs table schema"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/signinlogs"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-monitor/reference/tables/signinlogs" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SigninLogs table schema</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Expected result:</strong> a row matching the test account and sign-in time. No rows means you need to check the time range, identity, collection settings, destination, and ingestion delay. A missing table points to a collection or workspace issue before it points to a detection issue.</p> <h2 id="onboard-the-first-endpoint"> <a href="#onboard-the-first-endpoint" title="Onboard the First Endpoint">Onboard the First Endpoint</a> <a href="#onboard-the-first-endpoint" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Onboard the First Endpoint">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Intune enrollment and EDR onboarding</strong> are separate checkpoints. Connect Intune and Defender for Endpoint, enroll a supported Windows client, then assign an endpoint detection and response onboarding policy to its lab group. Entra registration alone does not establish either checkpoint.</p> <p>In Intune, check <strong>Endpoint security > Defender for Endpoint</strong>. If the connection is unavailable, enable the Intune connection in Defender’s endpoint advanced features. Follow the platform-specific steps in Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Intune and Defender integration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/microsoft-defender/configure-integration"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/intune/device-security/microsoft-defender/configure-integration" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Intune and Defender integration guide</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Checkpoint</th> <th>Evidence to capture</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Enrollment</strong></td> <td>Client appears in Intune with a recent check-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Policy assignment</strong></td> <td>Onboarding policy applies to the intended device group</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Sensor reporting</strong></td> <td>Defender shows onboarded status and recent telemetry</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Detection test</strong></td> <td>A documented test produces the expected security signal</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>For servers</strong>, enable the chosen Defender for Servers plan and its endpoint integration, then verify sensor deployment and reporting. Defender for Cloud also discovers machines before onboarding completes. Inventory presence alone is insufficient, as Microsoft explains in its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="resource discovery and onboarding guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/defender-for-cloud/integration-defender-for-endpoint" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >resource discovery and onboarding guidance</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="investigate-a-test-alert"> <a href="#investigate-a-test-alert" title="Investigate a Test Alert">Investigate a Test Alert</a> <a href="#investigate-a-test-alert" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Investigate a Test Alert">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Start with Microsoft’s documented EDR detection test</strong> on the lab endpoint. Follow the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="current test instructions"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-detection"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-endpoint/edr-detection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >current test instructions</a> </span> , including platform prerequisites and troubleshooting. Record the execution time before opening the alert queue.</p> <p>Treat the resulting alert as an investigation exercise. A security product’s title gives you a starting point. Your job is to establish what happened and support the disposition with evidence.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Triage:</strong> identify the alert source, device, account, and event time.</li> <li><strong>Inspect:</strong> review the process tree, command line, file details, and network activity available for the event.</li> <li><strong>Scope:</strong> search for related activity on the test identity and other lab devices.</li> <li><strong>Assess:</strong> explain whether the evidence matches the planned exercise or an unrelated event.</li> <li><strong>Respond:</strong> document the selected response, its impact, and the recovery steps. Perform supported containment only when the exercise requires it.</li> <li><strong>Retest:</strong> repeat the relevant test after changing a control and compare the evidence.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Do not manufacture missing results.</strong> If the alert fails to arrive, preserve the execution record and troubleshoot collection. If a control blocks the test before the expected event, document the prevention result.</p> <h2 id="test-identity-controls"> <a href="#test-identity-controls" title="Test Identity Controls">Test Identity Controls</a> <a href="#test-identity-controls" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test Identity Controls">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing</strong> places an attacker-controlled intermediary in a sign-in flow. The supplied runbook uses this scenario to motivate stronger authentication. For the first identity exercise, test policy behavior directly with your own unprivileged account.</p> <p>Begin by recording a legitimate sign-in and its authentication details. Review Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Entra risk detection reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-protection/concept-identity-protection-risks" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Entra risk detection reference</a> </span> before interpreting risk signals. Detection prerequisites and processing differ by signal. A new IP address or a failed sign-in does not guarantee an AiTM alert.</p> <p><strong>Passkeys (FIDO2)</strong> use credentials bound to the legitimate service rather than reusable codes entered into a relayed login page. Enable an appropriate passkey profile for the pilot group and register the method before enforcing a policy. Follow Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="passkey configuration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >passkey configuration guide</a> </span> for supported authenticators and restrictions.</p> <p><strong>Conditional Access exercise:</strong> create a policy targeting only the lab pilot group, exclude emergency access accounts, and select <strong>Require authentication strength > Phishing-resistant MFA strength</strong>. Start in <strong>Report-only</strong>, review its impact, then enable it.
