This adapts Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="administrator policy example"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-admin-phish-resistant-mfa"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-admin-phish-resistant-mfa" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >administrator policy example</a> </span> to a narrow test group.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Evidence to collect</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Report-only policy</strong></td> <td>Sign-in record showing how the proposed policy evaluates</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Enforced policy, weaker method</strong></td> <td>Fresh authentication requires a stronger method before access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Enforced policy, registered passkey</strong></td> <td>Successful sign-in satisfying the required strength</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Use fresh authentication for each comparison and inspect the policy details. Existing sessions complicate comparisons. <strong>Scope of proof:</strong> this exercise validates the authentication requirement. It does not demonstrate universal protection against endpoint compromise or theft of an existing session.</p> <h2 id="write-portfolio-evidence"> <a href="#write-portfolio-evidence" title="Write Portfolio Evidence">Write Portfolio Evidence</a> <a href="#write-portfolio-evidence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Write Portfolio Evidence">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A useful portfolio entry</strong> explains a decision another analyst is able to review. Include a short architecture description, the collection prerequisites, the event timeline, and the reasoning behind your response.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Exercise: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Date and UTC time window: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Lab scope and prerequisites: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Trigger and expected signal: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Observed alert or prevention: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Evidence and queries: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Affected identities and devices: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Disposition and reasoning: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Response and recovery: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Control change and retest: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Limitations and follow-up: </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Replace every field with your own observations. <strong>Sanitize exports:</strong> remove credentials, session material, personal information, and unnecessary identifiers before publishing screenshots or query results.</p> <p><strong>Resume example:</strong> “Built a Microsoft security lab, connected identity logs to Sentinel, investigated endpoint test alerts, and documented Conditional Access validation.” Use this wording only after completing those tasks. Put it under projects or practical training with the actual dates and scope.</p> <p>A lab demonstrates independent practice. <strong>Production SOC work</strong> also involves business impact, escalation, service commitments, and coordination with other teams. Explain which parts you practiced and which remain outside your experience.</p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Symptom</th> <th>First check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Workspace absent from Defender</strong></td> <td>Same tenant, Sentinel enabled, and onboarding role requirements</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>SigninLogs absent or empty</strong></td> <td>Diagnostic categories, destination workspace, fresh events, and time range</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Client absent from Intune</strong></td> <td>Enrollment prerequisites and enrollment status</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Device visible without telemetry</strong></td> <td>Actual onboarding state, sensor health, and outbound connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Onboarding policy unapplied</strong></td> <td>Assignment scope, device platform, and recent check-in</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>No identity risk alert</strong></td> <td>Signal prerequisites and recorded activity, without assuming deterministic detection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Unexpected access allowed</strong></td> <td>Report-only status, exclusions, resource scope, and existing session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Charges after shutdown</strong></td> <td>Allocation state and resources billed independently of compute</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Troubleshooting order:</strong> prove the event happened, prove collection worked, then investigate detection logic. Record each failure and fix in the project notes.</p> <h2 id="pause-or-remove-the-lab"> <a href="#pause-or-remove-the-lab" title="Pause or Remove the Lab">Pause or Remove the Lab</a> <a href="#pause-or-remove-the-lab" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pause or Remove the Lab">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Deallocation</strong> releases VM compute allocation. A guest operating system shutdown alone does not guarantee deallocation. Check Azure’s displayed power state and review Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="VM states and billing documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/states-billing"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/states-billing" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >VM states and billing documentation</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Retained resources</strong> still need review. Disks, snapshots, networking services, log retention, and user subscriptions have separate lifecycles. Set a reminder before each trial expires and verify the next usage report after cleanup.</p> <p>Before deleting the lab resource group, export the evidence you intend to retain and inspect its contents. <strong>Resource group deletion is destructive</strong> for contained resources. Tenant users, Intune policies, Conditional Access policies, subscriptions, and subscription-level security settings require separate cleanup where applicable.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Finish one documented investigation</strong> before adding another workload. Then add a server, an identity exercise, or a detection rule with a clear test condition. Track what the added component teaches and what it costs.</p> <p>Use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT home lab guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/" rel="follow me" >IT home lab guide</a> </span> for infrastructure practice and the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT resume guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/" rel="follow me" >IT resume guide</a> </span> to present the work. Keep the next project small enough to explain from setup through evidence and cleanup.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: The Most Common Types of Cyberattacks and How Defenders Catch Them
item.category: "Cybersecurity" , "Threat Detection" , "Blue Team" , "Security Operations" , "Career Development"
item.description: A practical tour of the most common cyberattack types, the evidence each one leaves behind in logs and telemetry, and how to practice detecting them in a home security lab.
item.content:encoded: <p>An <strong>attack type</strong> is a category of technique, not a single tool. Ransomware, phishing, and credential stuffing each name a method an adversary repeats against many targets with minor variations. Learning the categories gives you a mental index for the alerts you will meet on a security team.</p> <p><em>Individual malware families appear and disappear within months. The attack categories below have stayed stable for years, and each one leaves a recognizable trail in endpoint, identity, network, or email telemetry.</em></p> <!--more--> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Learn the pattern, not the payload.</strong> Attack categories change far slower than individual tools.</li> <li><strong>Every category leaves evidence.</strong> The detection work starts with knowing which telemetry records the activity.</li> <li><strong>Reproduce an attack to understand it.</strong> A home lab turns an abstract category into a recorded observation.</li> <li><strong>Write up what you found.</strong> A short investigation note proves the work and teaches you the evidence.</li> </ul> <h2 id="the-attack-types-at-a-glance"> <a href="#the-attack-types-at-a-glance" title="The Attack Types at a Glance">The Attack Types at a Glance</a> <a href="#the-attack-types-at-a-glance" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Attack Types at a Glance">#</a> </h2> <p>The table below lists the categories security teams meet most often. Each later section describes the category, its common variants, and the data a defender reviews to find it.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack type</th> <th>What it does</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Malware</strong></td> <td>Runs malicious software such as ransomware, spyware, and trojans</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Denial of service</strong></td> <td>Floods a service with traffic until legitimate users lose access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Phishing</strong></td> <td>Tricks a person into revealing credentials or running a malicious file</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spoofing</strong></td> <td>Disguises an attacker as a trusted system, sender, or address</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity-based attacks</strong></td> <td>Abuses stolen or forged credentials to act as a valid user</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Code injection</strong></td> <td>Inserts malicious code into an application to change its behavior</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Supply chain attacks</strong></td> <td>Compromises a trusted vendor, library, or update channel</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Social engineering</strong></td> <td>Manipulates a person into taking an unsafe action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Insider threats</strong></td> <td>Misuses access held by a current or former employee</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS tunneling</strong></td> <td>Encodes data inside DNS queries to move it past controls</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IoT attacks</strong></td> <td>Targets connected devices to pivot, spy, or join a botnet</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AI-powered attacks</strong></td> <td>Uses machine learning to generate content, impersonate people, or evade filters</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>A note on scope:</strong> these categories overlap. A phishing email often delivers malware, and a successful credential theft often precedes an identity-based attack. Treat the list as a set of lenses rather than rigid boxes.</p> <hr> <h2 id="malware"> <a href="#malware" title="Malware">Malware</a> <a href="#malware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Malware">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Malware</strong> covers any program built to harm, control, or profit from a system. The term spans ransomware, fileless malware, spyware, adware, trojans, worms, rootkits, keyloggers, and botnets.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Subtype</th> <th>Behavior</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Ransomware</strong></td> <td>Encrypts files and demands payment for the decryption key</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Fileless malware</strong></td> <td>Runs through built-in system tools and writes little to disk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spyware</strong></td> <td>Collects activity data without the user’s knowledge</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Trojan</strong></td> <td>Poses as legitimate software to gain execution</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Worm</strong></td> <td>Copies itself across hosts without user action</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Rootkit</strong></td> <td>Hides inside the operating system to keep persistent control</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> endpoint detection and response tools, or <strong>EDR</strong>, record process trees, command lines, file writes, and registry changes. Even a fileless attack produces process and script-block telemetry, because the operating system still launches the tools it abuses.</p> <hr> <h2 id="denial-of-service"> <a href="#denial-of-service" title="Denial of Service">Denial of Service</a> <a href="#denial-of-service" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Denial of Service">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A denial-of-service (DoS) attack</strong> floods a target with requests until legitimate users lose access. <strong>A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack</strong> repeats the same idea from many systems at once, which makes the traffic far harder to filter by source address.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Trait</th> <th>DoS</th> <th>DDoS</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Origin</strong></td> <td>One system</td> <td>Many systems</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Blocking difficulty</strong></td> <td>Moderate</td> <td>High, since the sources span many networks</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Typical impact</strong></td> <td>Lost availability</td> <td>Lost availability at larger scale</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> traffic volume against a baseline, connection counts per source, request-rate spikes, and error-rate changes. Availability monitoring often alerts before the security team sees the event.</p> <hr> <h2 id="phishing"> <a href="#phishing" title="Phishing">Phishing</a> <a href="#phishing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Phishing">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Phishing</strong> uses email, text messages, phone calls, or social media to push a person toward revealing credentials or running a malicious attachment. The category splits by target and channel.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Variant</th> <th>Target and channel</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Spear phishing</strong></td> <td>A specific person or team, usually by email</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Whaling</strong></td> <td>Senior or executive staff, often to move money or data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Smishing</strong></td> <td>Fraudulent text messages</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vishing</strong></td> <td>Fraudulent phone calls or voice messages</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> mail-gateway logs, URL detonation results, attachment analysis, and user reports. A report from a cautious employee is one of the highest-value signals on this list.</p> <hr> <h2 id="spoofing"> <a href="#spoofing" title="Spoofing">Spoofing</a> <a href="#spoofing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Spoofing">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Spoofing</strong> hides an attacker behind a trusted identity so a target accepts the connection, message, or address. The disguise buys time and defeats checks built around trust.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>What gets faked</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Domain spoofing</strong></td> <td>A lookalike website or email domain impersonating a real brand</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Email spoofing</strong></td> <td>The sender address on a message</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ARP spoofing</strong></td> <td>A local network address, to intercept traffic between two hosts</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results in mail headers, domain registration age, certificate mismatches, and duplicate address warnings on a local network.</p> <hr> <h2 id="identity-based-attacks"> <a href="#identity-based-attacks" title="Identity-Based Attacks">Identity-Based Attacks</a> <a href="#identity-based-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Identity-Based Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Identity-based attacks</strong> use a valid account rather than a defect in software. The attacker holds a working credential, so the activity sits close to normal use and blends into the background. This category drives a large share of the alerts a <strong>security operations center (SOC)</strong> handles each day.</p> <p><em>If you practice one category in a home lab, choose this one. The signals are rich, the exercises repeat, and the setup stays small.</em></p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>What happens</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Kerberoasting</strong></td> <td>Requests a service ticket, then cracks the encrypted password offline</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Man-in-the-middle (MITM)</strong></td> <td>Sits between two parties to read or alter a session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Pass-the-hash</strong></td> <td>Reuses a stolen password hash to open a new session</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Golden ticket</strong></td> <td>Forges a Kerberos ticket-granting ticket for broad domain access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Silver ticket</strong></td> <td>Forges a service ticket for one specific service</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Credential harvesting</strong></td> <td>Collects usernames and passwords in bulk</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Credential stuffing</strong></td> <td>Replays one set of credentials across many unrelated sites</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Password spraying</strong></td> <td>Tries one common password across many accounts</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Brute force</strong></td> <td>Guesses many passwords against one account</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Downgrade</strong></td> <td>Forces a connection into a weaker protocol version</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> sign-in records, failed-authentication counts, token anomalies, impossible-travel flags, and identity risk detections. <strong>Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing</strong> belongs here too, because the attacker steals a live session token rather than a password, and the replay from unfamiliar infrastructure trips the identity risk engine.</p> <hr> <h2 id="code-injection"> <a href="#code-injection" title="Code Injection">Code Injection</a> <a href="#code-injection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Code Injection">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Code injection</strong> places attacker-controlled code inside a vulnerable application so the application runs it as part of normal work. The application, not the attacker, carries out the harmful action.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Type</th> <th>Target</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SQL injection</strong></td> <td>A database query built from unvalidated input</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cross-site scripting (XSS)</strong></td> <td>A web page which renders attacker script in a visitor’s browser</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Malvertising</strong></td> <td>A legitimate ad slot filled with malicious code</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Data poisoning</strong></td> <td>A training set for an AI or machine learning model</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> web application logs, database query records, content security policy reports, and request patterns which differ from normal application use.</p> <hr> <h2 id="supply-chain-attacks"> <a href="#supply-chain-attacks" title="Supply Chain Attacks">Supply Chain Attacks</a> <a href="#supply-chain-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Supply Chain Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>A supply chain attack</strong> targets a trusted third party whose product or service reaches many customers. A <strong>software supply chain attack</strong> injects malicious code into an application, library, or update so every user of the product receives it. A <strong>hardware supply chain attack</strong> compromises a physical component before it ships.</p> <p><em>Modern software leans on third-party libraries, so one compromised dependency reaches far past the original vendor.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> software composition analysis, build-pipeline records, unexpected outbound connections from a trusted update, and integrity checks on shipped artifacts.</p> <hr> <h2 id="social-engineering"> <a href="#social-engineering" title="Social Engineering">Social Engineering</a> <a href="#social-engineering" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Social Engineering">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Social engineering</strong> uses psychological pressure to move a person toward an unsafe action. The attacker appeals to authority, urgency, fear, money, or trust.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>Approach</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Pretexting</strong></td> <td>Invents a believable scenario to gain trust</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Business email compromise (BEC)</strong></td> <td>Impersonates a trusted colleague to redirect a payment or share data</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disinformation</strong></td> <td>Spreads false narratives through social media and bots</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Quid pro quo</strong></td> <td>Offers a reward in exchange for information or access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Honeytrap</strong></td> <td>Builds a false relationship to extract money, data, or access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tailgating</strong></td> <td>Follows an employee through a secured door</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> email authentication results, unusual payment-change requests, helpdesk records, and physical access logs.</p> <hr> <h2 id="insider-threats"> <a href="#insider-threats" title="Insider Threats">Insider Threats</a> <a href="#insider-threats" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Insider Threats">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An insider threat</strong> is misuse of access by a current or former employee, contractor, or partner. Some insiders act with intent, driven by money or grievance. Others act through negligence, such as leaving credentials in a shared document.</p> <p><em>Negligent insiders appear more often than malicious ones in incident reports, and both call for the same detective control: compare access against a baseline for the role.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> data-transfer volume, activity outside normal hours, privilege changes, and bulk downloads from sensitive repositories.</p> <hr> <h2 id="dns-tunneling"> <a href="#dns-tunneling" title="DNS Tunneling">DNS Tunneling</a> <a href="#dns-tunneling" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="DNS Tunneling">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>DNS tunneling</strong> encodes data inside DNS queries and responses. Almost every network permits DNS, so the technique moves data past controls built to inspect web traffic.</p> <p><em>Detection leans on volume and shape. A single host sending thousands of queries to one domain stands apart from a normal baseline, and unusually long subdomains hint at an encoded payload.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> DNS query records, query length and volume per host, uncommon record types such as TXT, and lookups to domains registered days earlier.</p> <hr> <h2 id="iot-based-attacks"> <a href="#iot-based-attacks" title="IoT-Based Attacks">IoT-Based Attacks</a> <a href="#iot-based-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="IoT-Based Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>An IoT-based attack</strong> targets a connected device such as a camera, printer, thermostat, or sensor. Weak default credentials and rare firmware updates make these devices a common foothold. Once compromised, a device joins a botnet, leaks data, or becomes a route into the wider network.</p> <p><em>The 5G rollout adds connected devices at scale, and each new device is another target with a long patch cycle.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> device inventory, outbound connection patterns, abnormal data transfer from a device with a fixed role, and firmware version drift across a fleet.</p> <hr> <h2 id="ai-powered-attacks"> <a href="#ai-powered-attacks" title="AI-Powered Attacks">AI-Powered Attacks</a> <a href="#ai-powered-attacks" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="AI-Powered Attacks">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>AI-powered attacks</strong> apply machine learning to the attacker’s side of the work.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Technique</th> <th>Use</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Adversarial AI/ML</strong></td> <td>Manipulates training data or inputs to mislead a model</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dark AI</strong></td> <td>Applies AI and machine learning specifically to exploit vulnerabilities</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Deepfake</strong></td> <td>Generates realistic fake audio, video, or images</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AI-generated social engineering</strong></td> <td>Runs convincing chat or voice conversations at scale</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>A deepfake voice call or a fluent phishing chat raises the credibility of an old trick. The underlying technique stays familiar, which is why detection skills built on behavior outlast detection skills tied to one tool.</em></p> <p><strong>Where the evidence lives:</strong> content provenance signals, out-of-band verification for money or access requests, and behavioral anomalies around identity and payment changes.</p> <hr> <h2 id="mapping-attacks-to-telemetry"> <a href="#mapping-attacks-to-telemetry" title="Mapping Attacks to Telemetry">Mapping Attacks to Telemetry</a> <a href="#mapping-attacks-to-telemetry" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Mapping Attacks to Telemetry">#</a> </h2> <p>Each category feeds a different data source. The table below pairs them, which gives you a starting point for detection work.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Attack type</th> <th>Primary telemetry</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Malware</strong></td> <td>EDR process, file, and registry records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Denial of service</strong></td> <td>Network flow and availability monitors</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Phishing</strong></td> <td>Mail gateway and URL detonation records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Spoofing</strong></td> <td>Mail authentication and network address records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Identity-based</strong></td> <td>Sign-in and identity protection records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Code injection</strong></td> <td>Web application and database query logs</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Supply chain</strong></td> <td>Build pipeline and dependency inventory</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Social engineering</strong></td> <td>Mail, helpdesk, and physical access records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Insider threat</strong></td> <td>Data access and transfer records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS tunneling</strong></td> <td>DNS query records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IoT</strong></td> <td>Device inventory and outbound flow records</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>AI-powered</strong></td> <td>Identity, payment, and content provenance records</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Begin detection work with the telemetry column. A useful rule grows from a known data source and a known behavior, not from a tool name.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="practice-detecting-them-in-a-lab"> <a href="#practice-detecting-them-in-a-lab" title="Practice Detecting Them in a Lab">Practice Detecting Them in a Lab</a> <a href="#practice-detecting-them-in-a-lab" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Practice Detecting Them in a Lab">#</a> </h2> <p>A category stays abstract until you watch it happen. A home lab lets you generate the activity, capture the telemetry, and compare the alert against the raw record. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="career video on building a security operations center"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s3g8o7Np1_g"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s3g8o7Np1_g" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >career video on building a security operations center</a> </span> shows the full build for gaining job experience before being hired.</p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { yieldToMain(function () { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); }, "user-visible"); }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style> <p>Start with the identity category. Create a test user, enable sign-in logging, and run a sequence of failed and successful sign-ins. Then read the sign-in record and write down the fields which separate normal use from the exercise.</p> <p><strong>A repeatable exercise:</strong></p> <ol> <li><strong>Pick one category</strong> from the telemetry table above.</li> <li><strong>Reproduce a benign version</strong> of the activity against your own test system or account.</li> <li><strong>Collect the telemetry</strong> the category produces.</li> <li><strong>Write the detection idea</strong> as a rule, a saved search, or a query.</li> <li><strong>Test the rule</strong> against the exercise and confirm it fires on the intended behavior.</li> <li><strong>Record the limits</strong> of the rule, including the activity it misses.</li> </ol> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft SOC Home Lab guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/"> <a href="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/" rel="follow me" >Microsoft SOC Home Lab guide</a> </span> covers the environment build in detail: licensing, network segmentation, log collection, and identity control testing. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Mad Hat Cyber Range guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://madhat.io/pages/cyber-range-guide"> <a href="https://madhat.io/pages/cyber-range-guide" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Mad Hat Cyber Range guide</a> </span> expands the same idea into a workshop-grade build with an attack, detect, and defend exercise.</p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <center> <meta itemprop="name" content="simeononsecurity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/"> <a href="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/" title="simeononsecurity" target="_blank" class="markdown-btn" rel="follow" alt="simeononsecurity" > <button class="markdown-button"> Read the Microsoft SOC Home Lab Guide </button> </a> <p></p> </center> </span> <hr> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with one category and one exercise. Add a second category after you complete and document the first. The goal is depth on a single investigation, not a checklist of tools.</p> <ul> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft SOC Home Lab guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/"> <a href="/articles/microsoft-soc-home-lab-2026/" rel="follow me" >Microsoft SOC Home Lab guide</a> </span> </strong> builds the environment for these exercises.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Building an IT home lab"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/building-an-it-home-lab/" rel="follow me" >Building an IT home lab</a> </span> </strong> covers the infrastructure layer underneath a security lab.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT resume writing tips"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-a-job-in-it/it-resume-writing-tips/" rel="follow me" >IT resume writing tips</a> </span> </strong> shows how to present a documented lab as practical experience.</li> <li><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="The top five cyber attack vectors and mitigations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/the-top-five-cyber-attack-vectors-and-mitigations/"> <a href="/articles/the-top-five-cyber-attack-vectors-and-mitigations/" rel="follow me" >The top five cyber attack vectors and mitigations</a> </span> </strong> narrows the list to the vectors seen most often.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Source material:</strong> the attack categories and their subtypes follow <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="CrowdStrike’s overview of common cyberattacks"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/cybersecurity-101/cyberattacks/common-cyberattacks/"> <a href="https://www.crowdstrike.com/en-us/cybersecurity-101/cyberattacks/common-cyberattacks/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >CrowdStrike’s overview of common cyberattacks</a> </span> by Kurt Baker. Product and reference links point to Microsoft documentation.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Why Port Forwarding Doesn't Work on T-Mobile Home Internet
item.category: "Networking" , "Self-Hosted" , "Network Security"
item.description: Understand T-Mobile 5G Home Internet port-forwarding limits, carrier NAT, and practical options for reaching a home server without a public inbound port.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>T-Mobile’s consumer 5G Home Internet gateways</strong> do not offer configurable port forwarding. Adding a rule to a second router does not change the carrier gateway’s settings or create a public inbound route. T-Mobile also documents no bridge-mode toggle or adjustable network address translation (NAT) type. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="T-Mobile gateway settings"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.t-mobile.com/support/home-internet/connect"> <a href="https://www.t-mobile.com/support/home-internet/connect" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >T-Mobile gateway settings</a> </span> .</p> <p>This article covers <strong>cellular Home Internet</strong>. Treat fiber and business products as separate services with their own documented capabilities.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Identify the limit:</strong> distinguish a gateway feature from upstream address translation.</li> <li><strong>Inspect the path:</strong> record where each address and port belongs.</li> <li><strong>Compare alternatives:</strong> match client access and protocol requirements to a hosting method.</li> <li><strong>Write a decision:</strong> produce a connection plan with a test and fallback.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Audience:</strong> T-Mobile cellular Home Internet users trying to reach a home service from outside. <strong>Prerequisites:</strong> access to the server, its local network settings, and the supplied gateway’s status information. A second Internet connection is useful for the final remote test.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> 15–20 minutes to gather requirements and run local checks. Configuring a replacement access method takes additional time. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> beginner to intermediate. The objective is a justified connection choice, rather than another unused router rule.</p> <h2 id="why-a-local-port-rule-is-insufficient"> <a href="#why-a-local-port-rule-is-insufficient" title="Why a Local Port Rule Is Insufficient">Why a Local Port Rule Is Insufficient</a> <a href="#why-a-local-port-rule-is-insufficient" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why a Local Port Rule Is Insufficient">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Port forwarding</strong> maps incoming traffic at a router to an internal destination. For a home server to receive unsolicited Internet traffic, the route must work through every relevant upstream device. A successful local connection proves the server is reachable inside your network, not from outside it.</p> <p><strong>Carrier-grade NAT (CGNAT)</strong> adds address translation in the provider’s network. Subscribers share public IPv4 capacity, while the provider controls the outer translation. RFC 6598 reserves <strong><code>100.64.0.0/10</code></strong> for shared address space used in this kind of deployment. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="RFC 6598"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >RFC 6598</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Gateway support and carrier NAT are separate issues.</strong> T-Mobile’s support page establishes the gateway restriction. CGNAT explains why configuring your own router is also insufficient when upstream translation sits outside your control. A missing port-forwarding menu alone does not reveal the full carrier network design.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Change</th> <th>What it changes</th> <th>What remains unresolved</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Rule on a second router</strong></td> <td>Forwarding on your router</td> <td>Carrier gateway and upstream route</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Different DNS resolver</strong></td> <td>Name resolution</td> <td>Inbound connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Dynamic DNS hostname</strong></td> <td>A name following an address</td> <td>A usable inbound path</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Faster Wi-Fi</strong></td> <td>Local wireless performance</td> <td>Reachability from the Internet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Dynamic addressing</strong> means an address changes over time. It is distinct from sharing an address through NAT. T-Mobile documents dynamic addressing and no consumer Home Internet option to change it to static on this support page. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="T-Mobile connection limitations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.t-mobile.com/support/home-internet/connect"> <a href="https://www.t-mobile.com/support/home-internet/connect" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >T-Mobile connection limitations</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="trace-the-address-ownership"> <a href="#trace-the-address-ownership" title="Trace the Address Ownership">Trace the Address Ownership</a> <a href="#trace-the-address-ownership" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Trace the Address Ownership">#</a> </h2> <p>In a <strong>provider-NAT example</strong>, the path has several independent boundaries:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Remote client -> provider translation -> home gateway -> optional router -> server </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> provider controls home devices and local settings </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>An address visible to a website</strong> describes the connection reaching the website. It does not establish an inbound mapping to your server. The CGN requirements document discusses mappings in terms of subscriber identity, external address, port, and time. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="RFC 6888"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6888.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6888.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >RFC 6888</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Record the interface:</strong> distinguish your server’s local address, a second router’s WAN address, the cellular gateway’s reported address, and an external service’s observation. Here, <strong>WAN</strong> means the upstream side of a router. An address without its interface label is weak diagnostic evidence.</p> <p>Consider this <strong>illustrative observation</strong>, using documentation addresses for the public side:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation point</th> <th>Example reading</th> <th>Interpretation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Server LAN</strong></td> <td><code>192.168.50.10</code></td> <td>Local destination</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Second router WAN</strong></td> <td><code>192.168.12.20</code></td> <td>Another private network upstream</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>External IPv4 check</strong></td> <td><code>203.0.113.25</code></td> <td>Address seen outside</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Supported conclusion:</strong> the second router is behind another private network. <strong>Unsupported conclusion:</strong> its WAN reading proves the exact carrier translation arrangement. Inspect the cellular gateway separately if its status page exposes the relevant address.</p> <p><strong>Address-space clue:</strong> a provider-facing address in <code>100.64.0.0/10</code> is shared address space. Record which interface reports it. A private-network tool also assigning addresses from this range would make an unlabeled screenshot ambiguous. The range itself is defined by <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="RFC 6598"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6598.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >RFC 6598</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="check-the-local-service"> <a href="#check-the-local-service" title="Check the Local Service">Check the Local Service</a> <a href="#check-the-local-service" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check the Local Service">#</a> </h2> <p>For an <strong>HTTP dashboard</strong>, run this request from another Linux or macOS device on your home network. Replace the example address and port with your server’s values:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl --connect-timeout <span style="color:#ae81ff">5</span> --max-time <span style="color:#ae81ff">10</span> --output /dev/null --write-out <span style="color:#e6db74">'%{http_code}\n'</span> http://192.168.50.10:8080/ </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>--connect-timeout</code></strong> bounds connection setup. <strong><code>--max-time</code></strong> bounds the whole request. <strong><code>--output</code></strong> discards the response body, and <strong><code>--write-out</code></strong> displays the HTTP status. These options are documented in the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="curl manual"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html"> <a href="https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >curl manual</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Interpret the result:</strong> an HTTP response, including an authentication response, shows an HTTP endpoint answered on this route. Confirm its identity in your browser. A timeout does not identify the failing layer. Inspect the listening address, port, and host firewall next.</p> <p><em>This check applies to HTTP. A game using UDP needs a protocol-appropriate test.</em></p> <h2 id="choose-an-alternative-around-the-service"> <a href="#choose-an-alternative-around-the-service" title="Choose an Alternative Around the Service">Choose an Alternative Around the Service</a> <a href="#choose-an-alternative-around-the-service" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose an Alternative Around the Service">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Private access</strong> and <strong>public hosting</strong> have different requirements. Start by deciding who needs the connection and whether they are willing to install a client.</p> <p><strong>TCP</strong> transports an ordered stream over a connection. <strong>UDP</strong> transports individual datagrams. Hosting support must match the application’s transport, even when two services use the same numeric port.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Need</th> <th>Approach to evaluate</th> <th>Main constraint</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Your laptop reaching your home server</strong></td> <td>Tailscale private network</td> <td>Enroll devices and configure access rules</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A private browser dashboard</strong></td> <td>Cloudflare Tunnel plus Access</td> <td>Configure the hostname and identity policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A website for public visitors</strong></td> <td>Public hosting or an appropriate tunnel</td> <td>Review protocol, capacity, and service requirements</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A game server for ordinary game clients</strong></td> <td>Hosting with documented inbound port support</td> <td>Match the game’s TCP/UDP requirements</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Tailscale</strong> attempts a direct connection and supports relayed connectivity when direct communication fails. This avoids relying on a manually forwarded home port, although the resulting path affects performance. Read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale connection overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tailscale connection overview</a> </span> and our <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="relay explainer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/why-tailscale-uses-a-relay/"> <a href="/articles/why-tailscale-uses-a-relay/" rel="follow me" >relay explainer</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Cloudflare Tunnel</strong> establishes an outbound connection from your server. For a private dashboard, pair it with an Access policy. A published hostname without the policy does not add an identity check. See <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tunnel connectivity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/"> <a href="https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/networks/connectors/cloudflare-tunnel/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tunnel connectivity</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tunnel vs Access"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/cloudflare-tunnel-vs-access/"> <a href="/articles/cloudflare-tunnel-vs-access/" rel="follow me" >Tunnel vs Access</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>A VPN subscription alone</strong> does not specify an inbound hosting arrangement. Before buying any service, verify its supported protocols, exposed ports, authentication options, and restrictions. For a game server, ask specifically about the game’s required UDP ports.</p> <h2 id="what-about-ipv6"> <a href="#what-about-ipv6" title="What About IPv6?">What About IPv6?</a> <a href="#what-about-ipv6" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What About IPv6?">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>IPv6 addressing and inbound permission</strong> are separate requirements. IPv6 reduces dependence on IPv4 address translation, while stateful gateway filtering still controls incoming connections. RFC 6092 describes residential IPv6 filtering, including handling unsolicited traffic. It does not document the settings on your T-Mobile gateway. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Residential IPv6 security recommendations"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6092.html"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6092.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Residential IPv6 security recommendations</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Evaluate the complete route:</strong> the remote client needs IPv6 connectivity, the server needs an appropriate address and listener, and the network must permit the traffic. A successful IPv6 browsing test proves an outbound path. It does not prove an Internet client reaches your server.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>What it establishes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>An IPv6 address on the server</strong></td> <td>An address is assigned to an interface</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A successful outbound IPv6 request</strong></td> <td>This client reached an external service</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A remote application response</strong></td> <td>The tested inbound application route works</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Decision rule:</strong> choose IPv6 hosting only after confirming the complete inbound path and your clients’ compatibility. Avoid treating an address assignment as a substitute for a remote application test.</p> <h2 id="check-the-application-before-changing-the-network"> <a href="#check-the-application-before-changing-the-network" title="Check the Application Before Changing the Network">Check the Application Before Changing the Network</a> <a href="#check-the-application-before-changing-the-network" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check the Application Before Changing the Network">#</a> </h2> <p>Use these <strong>diagnostic steps</strong> to separate local failures from remote-access limits:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Local connection:</strong> confirm another home device reaches the server’s local address and intended port.</li> <li><strong>Service configuration:</strong> confirm the application listens on the expected interface and the host firewall permits the intended client.</li> <li><strong>Audience:</strong> decide whether access is private or public.</li> <li><strong>Remote test:</strong> test the chosen tunnel or private-network connection from a different Internet connection.</li> <li><strong>Performance:</strong> measure the actual workload after connectivity succeeds.</li> </ol> <p><strong>A failed local test</strong> needs attention before choosing a remote-access service. Port forwarding would not repair an application listening on the wrong interface.</p> <h2 id="work-through-a-hosting-choice"> <a href="#work-through-a-hosting-choice" title="Work Through a Hosting Choice">Work Through a Hosting Choice</a> <a href="#work-through-a-hosting-choice" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Work Through a Hosting Choice">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Scenario:</strong> you want to read a home dashboard while traveling, and two friends want to join a game server. Your dashboard is HTTP. The game requires UDP, and your friends want to use ordinary game clients without installing another network client.</p> <p><strong>Separate the requirements.</strong> A browser-based dashboard with a small identity list fits an authenticated web publishing arrangement. The game needs a public route supporting its required transport and clients. Solving the first requirement does not establish support for the second.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Requirement</th> <th>Reasoned choice</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Private dashboard in a browser</strong></td> <td>Evaluate Tunnel plus Access</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Personal access with enrolled devices</strong></td> <td>Evaluate a private overlay network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public UDP game clients</strong></td> <td>Evaluate hosting with documented UDP reachability</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Review question:</strong> would dynamic DNS make the game reachable through an unavailable inbound route? No. Updating a hostname does not create the required mapping or listener. Reject proposals addressing only the name while leaving the route unexplained.</p> <p><strong>Tradeoff to record:</strong> moving the game to external hosting changes recurring cost and administration. Asking friends to join a private network changes their setup requirements. Choose after confirming which constraint is negotiable.</p> <h2 id="build-a-connection-plan"> <a href="#build-a-connection-plan" title="Build a Connection Plan">Build a Connection Plan</a> <a href="#build-a-connection-plan" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build a Connection Plan">#</a> </h2> <p>Create a <strong>one-service plan</strong> with these fields:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Application and required TCP/UDP ports: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>People or devices needing access: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Client installation acceptable: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Local service test result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Inbound path available: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Chosen access method: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Authentication method: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Remote test and success criterion: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Fallback if the test fails: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Completion criterion:</strong> every step from the remote client to the application has an identified owner and supported mechanism. For a home tunnel, include the connector. For external hosting, include the host’s firewall and public listener. Leave unsupported assumptions visible until verified.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>For a browser dashboard, start with the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Cloudflare Tunnel setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/guides/how-to-setup-and-use-cloudflare-tunnels/"> <a href="/guides/how-to-setup-and-use-cloudflare-tunnels/" rel="follow me" >Cloudflare Tunnel setup guide</a> </span> and add Access. For broader service context, read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="T-Mobile Home Internet overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/other/t-mobile-home-internet-benefits-connectivity-features/"> <a href="/other/t-mobile-home-internet-benefits-connectivity-features/" rel="follow me" >T-Mobile Home Internet overview</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Why Tailscale Uses a Relay: Direct Connections, DERP, and Peer Relays
item.category: "Networking" , "Network Security" , "Self-Hosted"
item.description: Find out why Tailscale uses a relay, read status and netcheck output, and decide whether a DERP or peer-relay connection needs troubleshooting.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Tailscale uses a relay</strong> when devices have not established a direct connection. A brief DERP connection during startup is normal. Persistent relaying often reflects network address translation (NAT) or firewall conditions affecting the route between the devices. Direct, DERP, and peer-relay connections all retain WireGuard end-to-end encryption. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale connection types"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tailscale connection types</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Recognize the path:</strong> distinguish direct, DERP, and peer-relay connections.</li> <li><strong>Collect evidence:</strong> run peer-specific probes and network checks on both ends.</li> <li><strong>Analyze the pattern:</strong> compare device pairs and network conditions.</li> <li><strong>Choose a change:</strong> justify it with a measured workload and a retest.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> two enrolled, online devices and a terminal with the Tailscale command-line interface, or <strong>CLI</strong>, available. You need administrative access only if the investigation leads to configuration changes.</p> <p><strong>Estimated effort:</strong> five minutes for basic checks, then 15–20 minutes for the comparison exercise. <strong>Difficulty:</strong> beginner for observation and intermediate for network changes. Define the problem first, such as a slow backup or delayed terminal response.</p> <h2 id="direct-derp-and-peer-relay"> <a href="#direct-derp-and-peer-relay" title="Direct, DERP, and Peer Relay">Direct, DERP, and Peer Relay</a> <a href="#direct-derp-and-peer-relay" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Direct, DERP, and Peer Relay">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>tailnet</strong> is your Tailscale network. Its devices attempt direct UDP connectivity, with relays available when the direct path fails. Tailscale periodically rechecks its connection options. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Connection establishment"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Connection establishment</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Path</th> <th>Traffic route</th> <th>Typical implication</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Direct</strong></td> <td>Between the two devices</td> <td>Usually the preferred performance path</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DERP relay</strong></td> <td>Through Tailscale relay infrastructure</td> <td>Adds an intermediary when direct access fails</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Peer relay</strong></td> <td>Through a configured device in your tailnet</td> <td>An alternative relay under your administration</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>DERP performance</strong> depends partly on the extra route and shared service capacity. Tailscale documents throughput limits intended to share DERP resources fairly. There is no universal relay speed suitable for predicting your file-transfer time. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale performance troubleshooting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting/poor-performance-tailnet"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting/poor-performance-tailnet" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tailscale performance troubleshooting</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="understand-connection-negotiation"> <a href="#understand-connection-negotiation" title="Understand Connection Negotiation">Understand Connection Negotiation</a> <a href="#understand-connection-negotiation" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Understand Connection Negotiation">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>NAT traversal</strong> is the process of establishing a usable path across address-translating devices. Tailscale begins communication through DERP while negotiating a direct path. If direct connectivity fails, an available configured peer relay provides another option. Tailscale rechecks its options over time. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Connection establishment"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Connection establishment</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Hard NAT</strong> describes mapping behavior making traversal difficult. The conditions at both ends matter. Two devices behind different routers do not necessarily behave alike, even if both networks use private addresses. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Device connectivity"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/device-connectivity"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/device-connectivity" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Device connectivity</a> </span> .</p> <p>For <strong>a roaming laptop</strong>, the path to your home server might change after moving from home Wi-Fi to a hotel network. Record the network used during the observation. Yesterday’s direct connection is not evidence about today’s route.</p> <h2 id="check-your-current-connection"> <a href="#check-your-current-connection" title="Check Your Current Connection">Check Your Current Connection</a> <a href="#check-your-current-connection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Your Current Connection">#</a> </h2> <p>Replace <strong><code>home-server</code></strong> with your peer’s Tailscale name or address:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>tailscale ping home-server </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>tailscale status </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>tailscale netcheck </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong><code>tailscale ping</code></strong> probes connectivity to the named peer. <strong><code>tailscale status</code></strong> lists peers and connection details. <strong><code>tailscale netcheck</code></strong> reports conditions on the device running the command. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale CLI reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/tailscale-cli"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/tailscale-cli" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tailscale CLI reference</a> </span> documents these commands.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Output indicator</th> <th>Read it as</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong><code>direct</code></strong></td> <td>Traffic to this peer uses a direct path</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>relay</code></strong></td> <td>Traffic to this peer uses DERP</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>peer-relay</code></strong></td> <td>Traffic uses a configured peer relay</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>An initial DERP pong</strong></td> <td>Inspect subsequent results before deciding the path stayed relayed</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These labels come from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="connection-type documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/connection-types" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >connection-type documentation</a> </span> . <strong>Generate traffic first</strong>, then inspect the peer you care about. The commands above are examples, not captured results from a benchmark.</p> <h2 id="interpret-a-path-change"> <a href="#interpret-a-path-change" title="Interpret a Path Change">Interpret a Path Change</a> <a href="#interpret-a-path-change" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interpret a Path Change">#</a> </h2> <p>This <strong>illustrative sequence</strong> omits addresses and timings so you focus on the connection transition:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>First response: via DERP </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Later response: via a direct endpoint </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Status afterward: direct </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Interpretation:</strong> negotiation succeeded during this observation. The first response alone would have produced the wrong diagnosis. If later responses and status remain relayed, record a persistent relay for this device pair and test period.</p> <p><strong>Probe scope:</strong> a successful Tailscale ping establishes peer connectivity for its probe. It does not prove your dashboard, file service, or SSH daemon accepts application traffic. Test the failing application separately before declaring the problem solved.</p> <h2 id="what-netcheck-tells-you"> <a href="#what-netcheck-tells-you" title="What Netcheck Tells You">What Netcheck Tells You</a> <a href="#what-netcheck-tells-you" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What Netcheck Tells You">#</a> </h2> <p>Run <strong><code>tailscale netcheck</code> on both devices</strong>. Compare these fields against the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="device-connectivity reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/device-connectivity"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/device-connectivity" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >device-connectivity reference</a> </span> :</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Field</th> <th>Useful interpretation</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong><code>UDP</code></strong></td> <td>Whether the probe observed outbound UDP connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>MappingVariesByDestIP</code></strong></td> <td>Changing external mappings suggest difficult NAT traversal</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>IPv6</code></strong></td> <td>Whether this device has usable IPv6 connectivity</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>PortMapping</code></strong></td> <td>Whether a supported port-mapping mechanism is available</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>One field is not a verdict.</strong> An available mapping mechanism does not prove a particular peer path works. Likewise, a relay label does not identify which router caused it. Compare both endpoints and the actual ping results.</p> <p><strong>Carrier NAT</strong> is relevant when upstream translation is outside your control, as discussed in our <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="T-Mobile port-forwarding explainer"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/t-mobile-home-internet-port-forwarding/"> <a href="/articles/t-mobile-home-internet-port-forwarding/" rel="follow me" >T-Mobile port-forwarding explainer</a> </span> . Avoid assuming every connection behind carrier NAT has identical traversal behavior.</p> <h2 id="compare-three-device-pairs"> <a href="#compare-three-device-pairs" title="Compare Three Device Pairs">Compare Three Device Pairs</a> <a href="#compare-three-device-pairs" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Compare Three Device Pairs">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a <strong>third enrolled device</strong>, if available, to improve the evidence. The following is a hypothetical pattern, not a measured result:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Device pair</th> <th>Observed path</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Laptop to home server</strong></td> <td>DERP</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Laptop to another server</strong></td> <td>Direct</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Home server to another server</strong></td> <td>DERP</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Working hypothesis:</strong> prioritize the home server’s network for investigation because both observed paths involving it stayed relayed. This is a lead, not proof. Each pair negotiates independently, and the comparison server has its own network conditions.</p> <p><strong>Next observation:</strong> collect netcheck output on all three devices and repeat the laptop-to-home test from another network you control. If the path changes, record exactly which network changed. Avoid attributing the result to a particular firewall setting until you test it.</p> <p><strong>Review exercise:</strong> laptop-to-home is direct, but a file transfer remains slow. A relay explanation no longer matches this observation. Check the underlying upload connection, server load, storage, and application behavior before changing relay settings.</p> <h2 id="choose-a-targeted-change"> <a href="#choose-a-targeted-change" title="Choose a Targeted Change">Choose a Targeted Change</a> <a href="#choose-a-targeted-change" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose a Targeted Change">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with a <strong>comparison test</strong> on another network you control. If the same peer becomes direct, you have useful evidence about the original network path. Review its UDP restrictions and NAT arrangement before changing unrelated DNS or application settings.</p> <p><strong>Change one variable</strong>, rerun the checks, and measure the same workload. Record transfer direction, file size, elapsed time, and connection type. This separates an improved path from an unrelated change in server or storage load.</p> <p><strong>Firewall changes</strong> should follow the platform-specific guidance and the evidence you collected. Opening an application port to the public Internet does not itself improve Tailscale’s transport path. Keep changes limited to the required traffic and network you administer. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale firewall guidance"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/integrations/firewalls"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/integrations/firewalls" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Tailscale firewall guidance</a> </span> .</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Finding</th> <th>Change worth evaluating</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>UDP probe fails</strong></td> <td>Review outbound UDP restrictions on this network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mapping changes across destinations</strong></td> <td>Review NAT behavior on equipment you control</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Direct path, slow application</strong></td> <td>Investigate the host, underlying connection, and workload</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Working relay, acceptable experience</strong></td> <td>Keep the arrangement and document the baseline</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Prefer a measured improvement over changing settings solely to remove a relay label.</em></p> <h2 id="evaluate-a-peer-relay"> <a href="#evaluate-a-peer-relay" title="Evaluate a Peer Relay">Evaluate a Peer Relay</a> <a href="#evaluate-a-peer-relay" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Evaluate a Peer Relay">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>peer relay</strong> requires a suitable host, reachable UDP port, and an access policy permitting its use. Both the relay and participating clients require Tailscale 1.86 or later. Review supported host platforms before allocating a device. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Peer-relay requirements"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/features/peer-relay"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/features/peer-relay" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Peer-relay requirements</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Placement determines usefulness.</strong> A device behind the same inaccessible network boundary needs a reachable relay port before it helps other peers. Choosing a host geographically near the endpoints is insufficient without connectivity to it.</p> <p><strong>Maintenance tradeoff:</strong> someone must keep the relay online, updated, and adequately provisioned. For occasional administration with acceptable latency, compare this burden with the measured benefit. For repeated large transfers, measure the workload through the proposed relay before adopting it.</p> <h2 id="check-shared-traffic-effects"> <a href="#check-shared-traffic-effects" title="Check Shared Traffic Effects">Check Shared Traffic Effects</a> <a href="#check-shared-traffic-effects" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Shared Traffic Effects">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Aggregated traffic</strong> deserves attention when a subnet router or exit node carries several workloads through DERP. Tailscale documents situations where heavy relayed traffic delays latency-sensitive traffic sharing the connection. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hard-NAT troubleshooting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting/network-configuration/hard-nat-issues"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/reference/troubleshooting/network-configuration/hard-nat-issues" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Hard-NAT troubleshooting</a> </span> .</p> <p><strong>Comparison exercise:</strong> observe your interactive session before, during, and after a large backup. Keep the endpoint pair fixed and record the path each time. Delays appearing during the transfer justify investigating shared load, but do not establish its exact cause.</p> <p><strong>Choose the next test</strong> from the observation. Check link saturation and host load, then evaluate a direct path or separating latency-sensitive services if the topology supports it. Avoid treating a DNS symptom as automatic evidence of a DNS configuration error.</p> <h2 id="is-a-relay-an-exit-node"> <a href="#is-a-relay-an-exit-node" title="Is a Relay an Exit Node?">Is a Relay an Exit Node?</a> <a href="#is-a-relay-an-exit-node" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Is a Relay an Exit Node?">#</a> </h2> <p>An <strong>exit node</strong> routes a client’s general Internet traffic through a selected tailnet device. A relay carries traffic between Tailscale peers. Selecting an exit node does not guarantee a direct path to it. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Exit-node documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://tailscale.com/docs/features/exit-nodes"> <a href="https://tailscale.com/docs/features/exit-nodes" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Exit-node documentation</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="create-a-diagnostic-record"> <a href="#create-a-diagnostic-record" title="Create a Diagnostic Record">Create a Diagnostic Record</a> <a href="#create-a-diagnostic-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Create a Diagnostic Record">#</a> </h2> <p>Save a <strong>small before-and-after record</strong> for the actual problem:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Date and Tailscale versions: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Source and destination devices: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Networks used by each device: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Initial and settled connection paths: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Netcheck observations from both ends: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Workload, direction, and elapsed time: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Single change tested: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Retest result: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Decision to keep or revert: </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Completion criterion:</strong> the record links a specific symptom to observations, a hypothesis, and a measured retest. “Relay disappeared” is incomplete if the application is still slow. “The backup meets its time requirement through DERP” is a valid result if the requirement is explicit.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Record the path to your important peer and test the workload before changing network settings. For the separate question of who operates your coordination infrastructure, read <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Tailscale vs Headscale"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/tailscale-vs-headscale-comparison-guide/"> <a href="/articles/tailscale-vs-headscale-comparison-guide/" rel="follow me" >Tailscale vs Headscale</a> </span> .</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Flock Camera Detection Arms Race: What Changed in 2026
item.category: "Privacy Technology" , "Counter Surveillance" , "Open Source Projects" , "Digital Rights" , "Network Security" , "Security Research" , "Hardware Hacking" , "Privacy Tools"
item.description: Flock-You users are reporting zero detections on drives that used to catch cameras every time. Here is what changed in Flock Safety's hardware, why BLE and the old management AP both stopped working, how the open-source detection community responded, and an emerging infrared-based detection approach that skips WiFi entirely.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>If your Flock-You detector has gone quiet on a route that used to catch cameras every time, you are not imagining it, and your hardware probably is not broken.</strong> Flock Safety’s camera hardware and firmware have changed at least twice in the last year in ways that broke the community’s detection methods, and open-source researchers have had to reverse-engineer a new signature each time.</p> <p><em>This is a fast-moving story. The detection method and OUI list below reflect the <code>colonelpanichacks/flock-you</code> <code>main</code> branch as of September 2026.
