Check the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="GitHub repository"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you"> <a href="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >GitHub repository</a> </span> before assuming your device is defective.</em></p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); return; } var scriptTag = document.createElement('script'); scriptTag.src = '/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js'; scriptTag.setAttribute('defer', ''); scriptTag.setAttribute('type', 'module'); scriptTag.setAttribute('fetchpriority', 'low'); document.body.appendChild(scriptTag); } document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function () { yieldToMain(function () { loadLiteYouTubeScript(); }, "user-visible"); }); </script> <style scoped> .lite-youtube-fallback { aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; flex-direction: column; gap: 1em; padding: 1em; background-color: #000; color: #fff; text-decoration: none; } .lite-youtube-fallback::before { display: block; content: ''; border: solid transparent; border-width: 2em 0 2em 3em; border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style> <p><em>The video above, from Valleytech Custom Solutions, documents exactly the symptom this article explains: a routine war drive that suddenly returns zero detections across multiple firmware builds, on a route where cameras were reliably detected before, in a county where several previously-flagged cameras had physically disappeared.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="a-war-drive-that-suddenly-turned-up-nothing"> <a href="#a-war-drive-that-suddenly-turned-up-nothing" title="A War Drive That Suddenly Turned Up Nothing">A War Drive That Suddenly Turned Up Nothing</a> <a href="#a-war-drive-that-suddenly-turned-up-nothing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A War Drive That Suddenly Turned Up Nothing">#</a> </h2> <p>The pattern shows up the same way for almost everyone who reports it. A driver runs a route they have driven dozens of times. Their detector, running current firmware, has caught the same cameras before. Then, on one drive, it catches nothing. Not a single beep, not a single log entry, across every custom firmware build they try.</p> <p>The Valleytech video above describes exactly this: a daily route to the post office that always registered at least one Flock camera stopped registering any, and a second route past Micro Center that used to flag five cameras now shows only one still active, with the other four physically uprooted from their poles.</p> <p><strong>Two things were happening on the same timeline, and it is easy to confuse them:</strong></p> <ul> <li><strong>Cameras are being physically removed or relocated</strong> in some areas, which genuinely reduces the number of devices there are to detect.</li> <li><strong>The wireless signature the cameras broadcast has changed</strong>, which means even a camera still sitting on its pole will not trigger detection hardware running outdated firmware.</li> </ul> <p>Two separate GitHub issues on the <code>colonelpanichacks/flock-you</code> repository, filed months apart, document the second problem in detail. Reading them in order tells the story of how the community’s detection method has had to evolve twice already.</p> <hr> <h2 id="issue-20-the-management-ap-went-dark"> <a href="#issue-20-the-management-ap-went-dark" title="Issue #20: The Management AP Went Dark">Issue #20: The Management AP Went Dark</a> <a href="#issue-20-the-management-ap-went-dark" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Issue #20: The Management AP Went Dark">#</a> </h2> <p><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Issue #20"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/20"> <a href="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/20" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Issue #20</a> </span> </strong>, opened in January 2026, started with a familiar complaint: a user tested their device next to a known Flock camera, documented on DeFlock, and got nothing. Over the following weeks, more users piled on with the same result, from Florida to Indiana to Atlanta to the Midwest, using different hardware and different antennas.</p> <p>One commenter asked the question that turns out to matter most: <strong>had Flock changed something on their end, in a way that broke detection for everyone at roughly the same time?</strong></p> <p>The project maintainer, colonelpanichacks, eventually confirmed exactly that. <strong>Around December 2025, Flock deactivated the management access point their cameras used to broadcast.</strong> That AP was the original basis for wireless detection. When it disappeared, the community pivoted to Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) signals as a substitute. That substitute also stopped working reliably by spring 2026.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Detection surface</th> <th>Status</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Management WiFi AP</strong></td> <td>Deactivated by Flock, approximately December 2025</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>BLE beaconing</strong></td> <td>Stopped working reliably, spring 2026</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Cellular LTE uplink</strong></td> <td>Still in use for cloud upload, but not passively detectable</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Wildcard 802.11 probe requests</strong></td> <td>Current basis for detection (see below)</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Every custom firmware built around the old AP or BLE detection paths is now looking for a signal the cameras stopped sending. That is why a device that used to work goes completely silent without anything being wrong with the hardware.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="the-replacement-method-wildcard-probes-and-frame-fingerprinting"> <a href="#the-replacement-method-wildcard-probes-and-frame-fingerprinting" title="The Replacement Method: Wildcard Probes and Frame Fingerprinting">The Replacement Method: Wildcard Probes and Frame Fingerprinting</a> <a href="#the-replacement-method-wildcard-probes-and-frame-fingerprinting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Replacement Method: Wildcard Probes and Frame Fingerprinting">#</a> </h2> <p>The current <code>flock-you</code> firmware runs in dedicated 802.11 promiscuous mode. The radio never transmits and never joins a network. It only listens, hopping WiFi channels 11, 6, and 1 at a 250-millisecond dwell time to keep pace with how often the cameras themselves change channel.</p> <p><strong>A detection now requires all of the following to line up before the firmware alerts:</strong></p> <ol> <li>The frame is an 802.11 <strong>Management Probe Request</strong> (type 0, subtype 4).</li> <li>The <strong>SSID Information Element is present with length 0</strong>, meaning it is a wildcard probe rather than one asking for a specific network.</li> <li>The transmitter address (<strong>addr2</strong>) matches one of the known Flock OUI prefixes.</li> <li>The rest of the frame’s Information Elements match the fingerprint pattern the DeFlockJoplin community documented, based on Pintor and Atzori’s 2022 research on <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WiFi probe request IE fingerprinting"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10001618"> <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10001618" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WiFi probe request IE fingerprinting</a> </span> </strong>.</li> </ol> <p>This method is named <code>wifi_wildcard_probe_ie_sig</code> in the firmware. Field testing by the DeFlockJoplin community caught <strong>11 of 12 known cameras with only 2 false positives</strong> along their test route, the same field-verified baseline cited in the project’s own <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="hardware guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/"> <a href="/articles/flock-you-detection-project-counter-surveillance-hardware-guide-2026/" rel="follow me" >hardware guide</a> </span> </strong>. The 12th camera used an OUI that has since been added to the list below.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "caption": "Timeline diagram showing the Flock camera detection method evolving from a management WiFi access point, through Bluetooth Low Energy beaconing, to the current wildcard probe request and information element fingerprint, with a fourth stage showing emerging SSID, 5GHz, and MAC address evasion", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-12 23:23:19.87887913 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b511.605283579", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-12 23:23:19.87887913 +0000 UTC m=+511.605283579"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.ch/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.ch/flock-detection-arms-race-timeline-2026.webp" alt="Timeline diagram showing the Flock camera detection method evolving from a management WiFi access point, through Bluetooth Low Energy beaconing, to the current wildcard probe request and information element fingerprint, with a fourth stage showing emerging SSID, 5GHz, and MAC address evasion"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <hr> <h2 id="the-current-oui-list"> <a href="#the-current-oui-list" title="The Current OUI List">The Current OUI List</a> <a href="#the-current-oui-list" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Current OUI List">#</a> </h2> <p>The wildcard-probe fingerprint above only fires after the transmitter’s MAC address matches one of the OUI prefixes the community has confirmed against real Flock hardware. The list is maintained primarily by researcher <strong>@NitekryDPaul</strong>, with the 31st entry contributed by the <strong>DeFlockJoplin</strong> community after it caught a camera the original 30-entry list missed.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>70:c9:4e 3c:91:80 d8:f3:bc 80:30:49 b8:35:32 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>14:5a:fc 74:4c:a1 08:3a:88 9c:2f:9d c0:35:32 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>94:08:53 e4:aa:ea f4:6a:dd f8:a2:d6 24:b2:b9 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>00:f4:8d d0:39:57 e8:d0:fc e0:4f:43 b8:1e:a4 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>70:08:94 58:8e:81 ec:1b:bd 3c:71:bf 58:00:e3 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>90:35:ea 5c:93:a2 64:6e:69 48:27:ea a4:cf:12 </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>82:6b:f2 </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>This list is not static.</strong> The upstream research notes several prefixes that were tested and then demoted (one turned out to be a Sony media player, another an early placeholder that never matched anything). Two entries are flagged as low-confidence and one, <code>82:6b:f2</code>, is deliberately kept even though it is a locally-administered address, because filtering it out would have silently dropped a real, confirmed DeFlockJoplin detection.</p> <p><em>If you maintain your own firmware fork, pull the OUI list from the upstream <code>datasets/</code> folder rather than hardcoding a copy. The list changes as the research does, and a stale copy is a slow, silent way to start missing cameras again.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="issue-43-new-ssid-pattern-5ghz-and-mac-anti-fingerprinting"> <a href="#issue-43-new-ssid-pattern-5ghz-and-mac-anti-fingerprinting" title="Issue #43: New SSID Pattern, 5GHz, and MAC Anti-Fingerprinting">Issue #43: New SSID Pattern, 5GHz, and MAC Anti-Fingerprinting</a> <a href="#issue-43-new-ssid-pattern-5ghz-and-mac-anti-fingerprinting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Issue #43: New SSID Pattern, 5GHz, and MAC Anti-Fingerprinting">#</a> </h2> <p>Three months after Issue #20 closed, a second report arrived that describes what looks like a deliberate anti-detection countermeasure rather than an incidental firmware change. <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Issue #43"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/43"> <a href="https://github.com/colonelpanichacks/flock-you/issues/43" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Issue #43</a> </span> </strong>, filed in May 2026, is built on WiGLE wardriving data captured against a camera already confirmed on DeFlock, and it documents three findings none of the existing tooling accounted for.</p> <h3 id="finding-1-a-different-ssid-format"> <a href="#finding-1-a-different-ssid-format" title="Finding 1: A Different SSID Format">Finding 1: A Different SSID Format</a> <a href="#finding-1-a-different-ssid-format" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Finding 1: A Different SSID Format">#</a> </h3> <p>The documented Flock hotspot SSID has always followed the pattern <code>Flock-XXXXXX</code>. The camera in this report broadcast <strong><code>Flock Camera net.</code></strong> instead, a completely different naming convention. Anyone searching WiGLE for the <code>Flock-*</code> wildcard, as several researchers had been doing, would get zero results for this camera even though it was actively broadcasting.</p> <h3 id="finding-2-a-confirmed-5ghz-hotspot"> <a href="#finding-2-a-confirmed-5ghz-hotspot" title="Finding 2: A Confirmed 5GHz Hotspot">Finding 2: A Confirmed 5GHz Hotspot</a> <a href="#finding-2-a-confirmed-5ghz-hotspot" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Finding 2: A Confirmed 5GHz Hotspot">#</a> </h3> <p>The same camera broadcast simultaneously on <strong>2.4GHz channel 1</strong> and <strong>5GHz channel 157</strong>, using sequential MAC addresses on each band (<code>...9f:a2:de</code> and <code>...9f:a2:df</code>), which points to a single dual-band WiFi module assigning adjacent addresses to each radio rather than two unrelated devices. A separate, independent report from researcher nsm_barii had already logged a Flock probe request on 5GHz channel 149, so this is now two data points confirming 5GHz operation is real and not a one-off misconfiguration.</p> <p><strong>Every detection method described earlier in this article, including the current wildcard-probe firmware, only listens on 2.4GHz.</strong> A camera broadcasting exclusively (or primarily) on 5GHz is invisible to that hardware regardless of OUI list accuracy.</p> <h3 id="finding-3-locally-administered-mac-addresses-on-the-hotspot"> <a href="#finding-3-locally-administered-mac-addresses-on-the-hotspot" title="Finding 3: Locally Administered MAC Addresses on the Hotspot">Finding 3: Locally Administered MAC Addresses on the Hotspot</a> <a href="#finding-3-locally-administered-mac-addresses-on-the-hotspot" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Finding 3: Locally Administered MAC Addresses on the Hotspot">#</a> </h3> <p>Both captured MAC addresses have the <strong>locally administered bit set</strong>, meaning they were not assigned from Flock’s real IEEE-registered OUI block. The standard <code>flock-you</code> detection logic deliberately skips locally administered addresses, because that is the standard way to filter out MAC-randomizing phones and laptops.</p> <p><strong>That filter, which exists specifically to reduce false positives, means a Flock camera using a locally administered MAC on its hotspot interface gets filtered out by the exact same logic meant to clean up noise.</strong> The sequential last bytes on the two captured addresses rule out random generation, which is what makes this look like intentional, structured address assignment rather than coincidence.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Finding</th> <th>What still works despite it</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>New SSID format</strong> (<code>Flock Camera net.</code>)</td> <td>SSID pattern matching still works if the match pattern is broadened</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>5GHz operation</strong></td> <td>Nothing in current WiFi-only firmware, since detection only scans 2.4GHz</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Locally administered MAC</strong></td> <td>SSID pattern matching, since it does not depend on MAC address at all</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>SSID-based matching is the one method in this table that keeps working regardless of which band the camera uses or how its MAC address is assigned. That is the practical argument for adding broader SSID pattern support rather than relying on OUI matching alone.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="is-flock-deliberately-evading-detection"> <a href="#is-flock-deliberately-evading-detection" title="Is Flock Deliberately Evading Detection?">Is Flock Deliberately Evading Detection?</a> <a href="#is-flock-deliberately-evading-detection" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Is Flock Deliberately Evading Detection?">#</a> </h2> <p>Neither GitHub issue proves intent, and it is worth being precise about that. Issue #43’s own author raised it as an open question rather than a conclusion: is this consistent across Flock’s deployments, or specific to one firmware version on one camera?</p> <p>But look at the pattern across both issues together. A detection surface goes dark. The community finds a replacement. The replacement’s blind spots (2.4GHz-only scanning, OUI-based matching, filtering out locally administered MACs) line up closely with exactly the properties a new SSID format, a 5GHz radio, and a locally administered MAC address would exploit. <strong>That could be coincidence produced by an unrelated firmware upgrade cycle, or it could be a vendor tightening its own wireless footprint in ways that happen to break third-party detection as a side effect, intentional or not.</strong></p> <p><em>The most useful stance is not to argue which one it is. It is to build detection that does not depend on any single assumption holding forever, because on this project’s own two-year track record, none of them have.</em></p> <h3 id="visual-confirmation-powered-on-broadcasting-nothing"> <a href="#visual-confirmation-powered-on-broadcasting-nothing" title="Visual Confirmation: Powered On, Broadcasting Nothing">Visual Confirmation: Powered On, Broadcasting Nothing</a> <a href="#visual-confirmation-powered-on-broadcasting-nothing" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Visual Confirmation: Powered On, Broadcasting Nothing">#</a> </h3> <p><strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="A third Valleytech Custom Solutions short"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/sjI8FB0cLk0"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/sjI8FB0cLk0" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >A third Valleytech Custom Solutions short</a> </span> closes the loop on the “maybe the camera was removed” explanation.</strong></p> <script> function loadLiteYouTubeScript() { if (document.querySelector('script[src^="/p/jsdelivr/npm/@justinribeiro/lite-youtube@1.5.0/lite-youtube.js"]')) { console.log('Lite YouTube script is already loaded.'); } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style> <p>The creator returned to the same camera from the first video, at night, and visually confirmed its <strong>IR LEDs were still firing</strong>, meaning the unit was powered on and actively illuminating for night capture. At the same time, <strong>every custom firmware they tested logged zero legitimate hits</strong> against that camera. One alert did fire, but it was a confirmed false positive rather than a real detection. Nothing from the camera was reaching the wireless side at all.</p> <p><strong>This separates the two competing explanations cleanly.</strong> A camera that has been uprooted or relocated cannot explain a unit that is visibly powered on and illuminating at night. A camera that is live, illuminating, and still silent on every WiFi detection method is evidence the wireless signature itself has gone dark, not that the hardware disappeared.</p> <p>The creator also reported, after talking with other developers working on the same problem, that this was not an isolated result. <strong>Multiple people observed the same pattern at roughly the same time</strong>, which points toward a coordinated, nationwide change on Flock’s side rather than a local fluke at one camera. <em>That claim is anecdotal, based on informal conversation rather than a published dataset, but it lines up with the same December 2025 and spring 2026 windows described in Issue #20, and it is the kind of report that belongs in a new GitHub issue rather than staying as a comment thread.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="what-this-means-for-your-detection-hardware"> <a href="#what-this-means-for-your-detection-hardware" title="What This Means for Your Detection Hardware">What This Means for Your Detection Hardware</a> <a href="#what-this-means-for-your-detection-hardware" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What This Means for Your Detection Hardware">#</a> </h2> <p>If your device has gone quiet, work through this checklist before assuming it is broken:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Update your firmware first.</strong> If you are running anything older than the current <code>main</code> branch, you are likely still looking for the deactivated management AP or dead BLE beacons. Pull the latest firmware and reflash.</li> <li><strong>Confirm the camera is still there.</strong> Some of the “zero detections” reports turned out to be genuinely uprooted or relocated hardware, not a detection failure. Cross-reference against <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Flock Finder"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/flock-finder-alpr-surveillance-mapping-tool/"> <a href="/articles/flock-finder-alpr-surveillance-mapping-tool/" rel="follow me" >Flock Finder</a> </span> </strong> or <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DeFlock"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://deflock.org/"> <a href="https://deflock.org/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DeFlock</a> </span> </strong> before troubleshooting your device.</li> <li><strong>Slow down at intersections.</strong> The 250ms channel-hop dwell means a fast pass carries you past a camera’s detection window before your radio lands on the right channel. A 30-60 second stop catches far more cameras than a fast drive-by with a bigger antenna.</li> <li><strong>Report what you see.</strong> A confirmed zero-detection result next to a visually verified camera is exactly the kind of data point that turned into Issues #20 and #43. Open a new issue rather than assuming someone else already reported it.</li> <li><strong>Know the current limits.</strong> WiFi-only, 2.4GHz-only firmware will not see a camera that has moved to 5GHz or gone quiet on the bands it scans. That is a real gap right now, not a bug in your specific build.</li> </ol> <p><strong>None of this makes the hardware pointless.</strong> The OUI list and wildcard-probe fingerprint still catch the overwhelming majority of deployed cameras today. It means treating any detector, DIY or purchased, as a snapshot of the current arms race rather than a permanent solution.</p> <style> .flockyou-ad-lazy-image { display: block; max-width: 100%; the Infrared Flash Instead of the WiFi Signal</a> <a href="#a-parallel-approach-detecting-the-infrared-flash-instead-of-the-wifi-signal" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Parallel Approach: Detecting the Infrared Flash Instead of the WiFi Signal">#</a> </h2> <p>Wireless detection is not the only front in this arms race. <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="A separate follow-up video"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/mzpr6bslsYA"> <a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/mzpr6bslsYA" border-left-color: red; } .lite-youtube-fallback:hover::before { border-left-color: #fff; } .lite-youtube-fallback:focus { outline: 2px solid red; } </style> <p>Most ALPR cameras, Flock’s included, use <strong>infrared illumination to capture readable plates at night</strong>, the same reason ordinary security cameras work in the dark. That IR light is invisible to the human eye but visible to an image sensor that has not had its infrared-cut filter installed. <em>That single hardware detail, a missing IR-cut filter, is what turns an ordinary camera module into a Flock detector.</em></p> <h3 id="what-the-prototype-looks-like"> <a href="#what-the-prototype-looks-like" title="What the Prototype Looks Like">What the Prototype Looks Like</a> <a href="#what-the-prototype-looks-like" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Prototype Looks Like">#</a> </h3> <p>The approach documented in the video went through several iterations before landing on a workable combination:</p> <ul> <li><strong>First attempt</strong>: dedicated IR photodiode receivers. Technically workable, but the parts were too expensive to be a practical DIY option.</li> <li><strong>Second attempt</strong>: a <strong>Jetson Nano paired with a Raspberry Pi camera module</strong>. This proved the concept worked, but the hardware cost and power draw made it impractical for a handheld or vehicle-mounted build.</li> <li><strong>Current build</strong>: an <strong>ESP32-based camera module without an IR-cut lens</strong>. The creator tested an <strong>ESP32-CAM</strong> and an <strong>M5Stack S3 Cam</strong> before settling on the <strong>Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 Sense</strong>, paired with a <strong>Seeed XIAO GNSS module built on the Quectel L76K chip</strong> for GPS-tagging detections, the same GPS-wardriving pattern the WiFi-based <code>flock-you</code> dashboard already uses.</li> </ul> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Requirement</th> <th>Why it matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>No IR-cut filter on the camera module</strong></td> <td>The filter that makes ordinary photos look color-correct also blocks the exact light this method needs to see</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>A camera rather than a photodiode</strong></td> <td>Photodiode receivers capable of isolating the signal were too expensive to be practical for a DIY build</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GPS logging</strong></td> <td>Matches detections to a location the same way the WiFi firmware’s Flask dashboard does</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="the-cameras-blink-pattern"> <a href="#the-cameras-blink-pattern" title="The Camera’s Blink Pattern">The Camera’s Blink Pattern</a> <a href="#the-cameras-blink-pattern" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Camera’s Blink Pattern">#</a> </h3> <p>The premise depends on the illuminator flashing in a detectable, repeating pattern rather than staying continuously lit. The creator reported a <strong>self-measured timing of roughly 20 milliseconds on and 80 milliseconds off, a 100-millisecond period, which works out to a 20% duty cycle at 10Hz</strong>, and was explicit that this figure is unverified and could be wrong. <em>Treat that specific number as a starting point for your own measurement, not a confirmed spec, since Flock has never published it and the creator did not claim certainty either.</em></p> <h3 id="where-the-project-stands"> <a href="#where-the-project-stands" title="Where the Project Stands">Where the Project Stands</a> <a href="#where-the-project-stands" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where the Project Stands">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>This is an early, DIY-only prototype, not a finished product.</strong> The creator described the software as “vibe coded” and still in progress, with a buzzer for audible alerts planned but not yet added, and no packaged board equivalent to the OUI-SPY hardware. The current version still requires a <strong>human to visually confirm</strong> that a flagged detection is an actual camera rather than another IR-emitting light source, so it works as a screening tool rather than a fully automated one.</p> <p><em>This is a genuinely different detection surface than everything else in this article. It does not depend on WiFi, 2.4GHz or 5GHz, OUI matching, or MAC address behavior at all, which means none of the evasion techniques described in Issue #43 apply to it. That also means it inherits its own limitations: line of sight, daylight interference, and a duty cycle assumption that has not been independently confirmed.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="what-the-community-is-doing-about-it"> <a href="#what-the-community-is-doing-about-it" title="What the Community Is Doing About It">What the Community Is Doing About It</a> <a href="#what-the-community-is-doing-about-it" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What the Community Is Doing About It">#</a> </h2> <p>The response to both issues followed the same pattern that has kept this project useful for two years: someone reports a gap, someone else contributes the fix, and the fix ships as an update rather than sitting in a backlog.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Issue #20</strong> ended with a confirmed root cause and a firmware rewrite around the wildcard-probe signature, credited to the DeFlockJoplin community’s field research.</li> <li><strong>Issue #43</strong> remains open as of this writing, with the SSID pattern-matching suggestion still pending implementation. <em>If you want to help close that gap, the fix (adding <code>Flock Camera</code> as an additional match pattern) is a small, well-scoped contribution for anyone comfortable with the firmware’s match logic.</em></li> <li>The underlying OUI dataset is versioned and dated in the repository, with demoted and low-confidence entries documented rather than silently dropped, so anyone forking the project sees exactly what changed and why.</li> </ul> <p><em>This is the practical case for open-source detection tooling over a closed-source alternative. A proprietary detector cannot be patched by the person who found the gap. This one already has been, twice.</em></p> <hr> <h2 id="conclusion-detection-is-a-moving-target-not-a-fixed-answer"> <a href="#conclusion-detection-is-a-moving-target-not-a-fixed-answer" title="Conclusion: Detection Is a Moving Target, Not a Fixed Answer">Conclusion: Detection Is a Moving Target, Not a Fixed Answer</a> <a href="#conclusion-detection-is-a-moving-target-not-a-fixed-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Conclusion: Detection Is a Moving Target, Not a Fixed Answer">#</a> </h2> <p>A silent detector on a route that used to catch cameras is not proof your hardware failed. It is evidence that the wireless signature it was built to recognize has changed, again, in a pattern that has now repeated twice inside a single year. The <strong>management AP, BLE beaconing, and now potentially the 2.4GHz-only, OUI-only assumptions baked into the current firmware</strong> have each had a limited shelf life.</p> <p><strong>The fix has never been to give up on wireless detection.</strong> It has been to keep the detection method’s assumptions visible, documented, and open to correction the next time a report like Issue #20 or Issue #43 comes in. That is the argument for open-source firmware over any closed alternative: the fix ships as soon as the community finds the gap, not on the vendor’s schedule.</p> <h3 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h3> <ul> <li><strong>Two documented detection surfaces have already gone dark</strong>: the management WiFi AP (deactivated around December 2025) and BLE beaconing (unreliable by spring 2026).</li> <li><strong>The current method, wildcard probe requests plus OUI and IE fingerprint matching, has a field-verified 11-of-12 detection rate</strong>, but it is WiFi-only and 2.4GHz-only.</li> <li><strong>A pending report describes a new SSID format, a confirmed 5GHz hotspot, and locally-administered MAC addresses</strong> that the current OUI-based, 2.4GHz-only method cannot see.</li> <li><strong>A separate, non-wireless approach is emerging</strong>: an ESP32 camera module with its IR-cut filter removed spots a Flock camera’s infrared illuminator, a detection surface that ignores WiFi entirely and is immune to every evasion technique above.</li> <li><strong>Visual confirmation backs the wireless silence up</strong>: a camera visibly powered on and illuminating at night still logged zero legitimate WiFi hits, which rules out “the camera was removed” as the explanation for that specific unit.</li> <li><strong>A zero-detection result on a known camera does not automatically mean your hardware is broken.</strong> Update your firmware first, then confirm the camera is physically still there.</li> <li><strong>This is an open-source project that keeps shipping fixes as the community finds gaps.</strong> Read the GitHub item.title: Meshtastic vs MeshCore vs Reticulum
item.category: "LoRa" , "Mesh Networking" , "Off-Grid Communications" , "Emergency Communications" , "Ham Radio" , "Open Source" , "Disaster Preparedness" , "Wireless Networks" , "Privacy" , "Networking"
item.description: A practical comparison of Meshtastic, MeshCore, and Reticulum for off-grid and community mesh networking. Covers routing architecture, hop limits and airtime, static infrastructure versus roaming nodes, and when transport-independent networking with Reticulum genuinely solves a real problem.
item.content:encoded: <h2 id="the-short-answer"> <a href="#the-short-answer" title="The Short Answer">The Short Answer</a> <a href="#the-short-answer" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Short Answer">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>These three projects do not all solve the same problem.</strong> Meshtastic and MeshCore are LoRa mesh networking systems with different routing philosophies. Reticulum is broader. It is a transport-independent networking layer running over LoRa, packet radio, Wi-Fi, Ethernet, serial links, and the internet at the same time.</p> <p><strong>The right question is not “which is best?”</strong> It is “which architecture fits the network I am trying to build?”</p> <p><em>Meshtastic fits ad hoc and roaming use.</em> <strong>MeshCore fits deliberately built, fixed infrastructure.</strong> <strong>Reticulum fits networks needing to bridge different transports or connect otherwise separate networks.</strong> Most people building one regional LoRa mesh only need one of the first two.</p> <hr> <h2 id="define-the-network-you-are-building"> <a href="#define-the-network-you-are-building" title="Define the Network You Are Building">Define the Network You Are Building</a> <a href="#define-the-network-you-are-building" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define the Network You Are Building">#</a> </h2> <p>Before comparing protocols, write down what the network needs to do. A useful target for most community and emergency-communications deployments looks like this:</p> <ul> <li><strong>License-free operation</strong>, so anyone participates without a ham license</li> <li><strong>Low-cost hardware</strong> affordable for a community to deploy at scale</li> <li><strong>Low power consumption</strong>, ideally solar or battery sustainable</li> <li><strong>Long-range communication</strong> without cellular or internet dependency</li> <li><strong>Infrastructure independence</strong> from the grid, ISPs, and carriers</li> <li><strong>Easy enough for non-radio experts</strong> to set up and use</li> <li><strong>Suitable for community deployment</strong>, not only a single operator’s basement</li> <li><strong>Able to grow beyond a handful of nodes</strong> without falling apart</li> <li><strong>Useful during infrastructure failures</strong>, when cell towers and internet are down</li> <li><strong>Reliable delivery matters more than record-setting distance</strong></li> </ul> <p>Keep this list in mind through the rest of the article. Every architectural tradeoff below gets evaluated against it.</p> <hr> <h2 id="meshtastic"> <a href="#meshtastic" title="Meshtastic">Meshtastic</a> <a href="#meshtastic" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Meshtastic">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Meshtastic</strong> is the most mature and widely deployed option here. It gets a lot right for the median user.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Mature ecosystem</strong> with years of active development</li> <li><strong>Large user community</strong>, active Discord, and extensive documentation</li> <li><strong>Broad hardware support</strong> across LILYGO, Heltec, RAK, and Seeed boards</li> <li><strong>Good mobile applications</strong> for iOS and Android</li> <li><strong>Easy entry point</strong>, first-time setup takes under 20 minutes</li> <li><strong>Strong support for portable and roaming users</strong> who join and leave the mesh unpredictably</li> <li><strong>GPS and telemetry features</strong> with a developed ecosystem around them</li> <li><strong>Existing deployments</strong> in most metro areas make adoption easier, since you are joining a network instead of building one from nothing</li> </ul> <p>For a full breakdown of Meshtastic’s routing, hardware compatibility, and setup process against MeshCore specifically, see the <strong> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MeshCore vs Meshtastic comparison guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/meshcore-vs-meshtastic-comparison-guide/"> <a href="/articles/meshcore-vs-meshtastic-comparison-guide/" rel="follow me" >MeshCore vs Meshtastic comparison guide</a> </span> </strong>. This article focuses on the architectural question mattering most for larger deployments: <strong>managed flooding and hop limits.</strong></p> <h3 id="managed-flooding-and-why-hop-limits-matter"> <a href="#managed-flooding-and-why-hop-limits-matter" title="Managed Flooding and Why Hop Limits Matter">Managed Flooding and Why Hop Limits Matter</a> <a href="#managed-flooding-and-why-hop-limits-matter" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Managed Flooding and Why Hop Limits Matter">#</a> </h3> <p>Meshtastic broadcasts use <strong>managed flooding</strong>. When a node sends a message, every node hearing it rebroadcasts the packet, up to a configured hop limit. No node needs to know the network topology. New nodes join with zero configuration, and dead nodes get bypassed automatically since the flood routes around them.</p> <p>The default hop limit is <strong>3</strong>. The maximum is <strong>7</strong>. The framing worth avoiding is “Meshtastic only goes seven hops.” <em>The real question is what raising this number costs you.</em></p> <p>Each additional hop means every node within range of the message rebroadcasts it again. More forwarding produces:</p> <ul> <li><strong>More airtime</strong> consumed per message</li> <li><strong>More duplicate transmissions</strong>, since every node in range of a rebroadcast repeats it</li> <li><strong>More contention</strong> for the shared channel</li> <li><strong>Greater collision risk</strong> as more radios try to transmit in the same window</li> <li><strong>Higher battery consumption</strong> on every node receiving and retransmitting</li> <li><strong>Less available channel capacity</strong> for actual message traffic</li> </ul> <p>LoRa capacity is bounded by airtime and regional duty cycle limits, not by node count. A network with ten chatty nodes sending frequent GPS and telemetry broadcasts saturates a channel fifty quiet sensor nodes would never touch. This is why a dense mesh with a high hop limit degrades faster than the same node count spread across a lower hop limit and disciplined telemetry intervals. <strong>Meshtastic 2.6 improved this for direct messages</strong> by switching to next-hop routing after route discovery, so point-to-point traffic no longer floods the whole hop radius. Broadcasts still flood.</p> <p>For a small or medium hiking-club-sized mesh, this rarely matters. For a <strong>regional network meant to cover a city or a multi-town area</strong>, it becomes the central design constraint.</p> <hr> <h2 id="meshcore"> <a href="#meshcore" title="MeshCore">MeshCore</a> <a href="#meshcore" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="MeshCore">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>MeshCore</strong> takes a different architectural bet: instead of treating every device as an equal participant in message propagation, it builds a deliberate infrastructure layer and routes traffic toward it.</p> <h3 id="node-roles"> <a href="#node-roles" title="Node Roles">Node Roles</a> <a href="#node-roles" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Node Roles">#</a> </h3> <p>MeshCore deployments are built around distinct roles rather than one flat set of equivalent nodes:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Companion or client nodes</strong> carry a LoRa radio paired to a phone or laptop and talk through nearby infrastructure when it is present</li> <li><strong>Repeaters</strong> exist specifically to forward traffic between clients and other infrastructure, and do most of the actual routing work</li> <li><strong>Room servers</strong> (optional) hold group conversations and deliver stored messages to clients when they reconnect</li> </ul> <p>Route discovery happens first, then traffic moves through the discovered path toward its destination rather than fanning out to every node in range. Channel occupancy scales with active conversations, not total node count, which is a meaningfully different growth curve than Meshtastic’s flooding model.</p> <h3 id="why-this-fits-static-infrastructure"> <a href="#why-this-fits-static-infrastructure" title="Why This Fits Static Infrastructure">Why This Fits Static Infrastructure</a> <a href="#why-this-fits-static-infrastructure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why This Fits Static Infrastructure">#</a> </h3> <p><em>This is the core argument for MeshCore.</em> Meshtastic’s flooding model has real advantages for ad hoc and roaming networks: no planning required, no infrastructure to maintain, and graceful handling of nodes coming and going. MeshCore’s routing model has the advantage when <strong>users intentionally deploy infrastructure</strong>.</p> <p>A network built around known, elevated repeaters gives you the ability to design coverage on purpose, rather than depending on whichever nodes happen to be in range of each other on a given day. This difference matters for:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Permanent rooftop nodes</strong> with reliable power</li> <li><strong>Towers</strong> and existing communications infrastructure</li> <li><strong>Solar repeaters</strong> at unattended sites</li> <li><strong>Mountain or elevated relay sites</strong></li> <li><strong>Community-owned infrastructure</strong> shared across multiple groups</li> <li><strong>Regional networks</strong> spanning more than a single neighborhood</li> <li><strong>Emergency communications</strong> where predictable coverage matters more than flexibility</li> </ul> <p>Tie this back to RF fundamentals: <strong>reliable links between properly placed infrastructure matter more than maximizing antenna gain, transmit power, or theoretical range.</strong> A protocol built around dedicated repeaters rewards you for doing the RF engineering work of siting those repeaters well. A protocol built around flooding rewards you less for this work, since every node does roughly the same job regardless of where you put it.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-roaming-node-argument-and-why-it-is-not-free"> <a href="#the-roaming-node-argument-and-why-it-is-not-free" title="The Roaming-Node Argument, and Why It Is Not Free">The Roaming-Node Argument, and Why It Is Not Free</a> <a href="#the-roaming-node-argument-and-why-it-is-not-free" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Roaming-Node Argument, and Why It Is Not Free">#</a> </h2> <p>A common suggestion goes like this: <em>“Meshtastic is better for roaming nodes, MeshCore is better for static nodes, so run Meshtastic for users and MeshCore as the backbone.”</em></p> <p>This sounds attractive on paper. In practice, mixing the two does not automatically produce the strengths of both, since <strong>Meshtastic and MeshCore use different routing and network architectures, and they do not exchange messages with each other.</strong> Bridging them means adding a translation layer between two incompatible systems, not simply picking the best parts of each.</p> <p>Once you bridge them, you are running:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Two separate networks</strong>, each with its own topology and behavior</li> <li><strong>Two routing models</strong> sharing no state</li> <li><strong>A translation layer</strong> between them, requiring ongoing build and maintenance</li> <li><strong>More infrastructure</strong> to host the bridge</li> <li><strong>More configuration</strong> across two firmware ecosystems instead of one</li> <li><strong>More failure points</strong>, since the bridge itself fails independently of either mesh</li> <li><strong>Harder troubleshooting</strong>, since a delivery failure lives in either network or in the bridge connecting them</li> </ul> <p>Before adopting this design, ask a direct question: <strong>does the added complexity solve a problem a single, well-tuned mesh protocol fails to solve on its own?</strong> Often the honest answer is a properly configured MeshCore deployment with a few roaming-friendly companion nodes, or a Meshtastic deployment with a couple of well-placed high-hop-limit relays, delivers most of the practical benefit without running two networks glued together.</p> <hr> <h2 id="reticulum"> <a href="#reticulum" title="Reticulum">Reticulum</a> <a href="#reticulum" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reticulum">#</a> </h2> <p>Reticulum deserves its own category rather than a slot as “a third LoRa mesh option,” because it is not primarily a LoRa mesh protocol at all. <strong>Its defining feature is transport independence.</strong></p> <p>Reticulum is a cryptography-based networking stack. It does not use source addresses, so packets carry no information about where they originated. Every address is self-sovereign: once generated, it becomes globally reachable within seconds to minutes and stays reachable even after physically moving to a different part of the network. All communication is encrypted by default with ephemeral keys and forward secrecy. Reticulum drops unencrypted packets rather than deliver them. None of this requires kernel drivers. It runs in userland on any system running Python 3, including a Raspberry Pi Zero.</p> <p>The interfaces Reticulum supports include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>LoRa</strong>, using RNode-compatible hardware (a defined open-source LoRa transceiver design, buildable, flashable onto common boards, or purchased ready-made)</li> <li><strong>Packet radio</strong>, through any TNC running in KISS mode, which fits VHF and UHF amateur radio well</li> <li><strong>Wi-Fi and wired Ethernet</strong>, using automatic peer discovery with no router or DHCP server required</li> <li><strong>Serial links</strong>, for direct device-to-device connections</li> <li><strong>TCP and UDP over existing IP networks</strong>, including the internet</li> <li><strong>The I2P network</strong>, and custom interfaces for anything else with a Python bridge</li> </ul> <p>On top of Reticulum sit applications like <strong>LXMF</strong> (a delay-tolerant messaging protocol), and end-user tools such as <strong>Sideband</strong>, <strong>NomadNet</strong>, and community <strong>MeshChat</strong> clients, which give Reticulum networks a messaging and browsing layer comparable to what Meshtastic and MeshCore ship out of the box.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "caption": "Diagram showing Reticulum connecting a LoRa mesh, a packet radio network, and an internet link into a single addressable, encrypted network", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-12 23:23:19.883628684 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b511.610033153", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-12 23:23:19.883628684 +0000 UTC m=+511.610033153"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.ch/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.ch/reticulum-transport-independent-heterogeneous-network.webp" alt="Diagram showing Reticulum connecting a LoRa mesh, a packet radio network, and an internet link into a single addressable, encrypted network"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <h3 id="where-reticulum-makes-sense"> <a href="#where-reticulum-makes-sense" title="Where Reticulum Makes Sense">Where Reticulum Makes Sense</a> <a href="#where-reticulum-makes-sense" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Reticulum Makes Sense">#</a> </h3> <p>Reticulum’s value shows up clearly in a heterogeneous setup, for example:</p> <p><strong>LoRa mesh to Reticulum node to IP link to Reticulum node to radio network</strong></p> <p>Here Reticulum is doing something neither Meshtastic nor MeshCore does: connecting two otherwise distinct communications systems into one addressable network. This is a real and specific requirement, not a generic upgrade. Good fits include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Linking geographically separated networks</strong> lacking a direct radio path between them</li> <li><strong>Bridging different physical transports</strong>, such as a LoRa mesh on one end and a packet radio network on the other</li> <li><strong>Radio-to-IP gateways</strong> handing traffic between a field radio network and the internet</li> <li><strong>Experimental and research networking</strong>, where the flexibility to mix transports matters more than deployment simplicity</li> <li><strong>Networks where no single transport covers the entire requirement</strong>, so something has to stitch the pieces together</li> </ul> <h3 id="where-reticulum-adds-unnecessary-complexity"> <a href="#where-reticulum-adds-unnecessary-complexity" title="Where Reticulum Adds Unnecessary Complexity">Where Reticulum Adds Unnecessary Complexity</a> <a href="#where-reticulum-adds-unnecessary-complexity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Where Reticulum Adds Unnecessary Complexity">#</a> </h3> <p>If everyone in a deployment uses compatible LoRa hardware and the actual goal is <strong>one regional LoRa mesh</strong>, adding Reticulum on top provides little benefit and a real cost. Every additional layer in a network stack means more:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Configuration</strong> to get right and keep consistent across nodes</li> <li><strong>Software</strong> to install, update, and troubleshoot</li> <li><strong>Hardware</strong> in some configurations, depending on how interfaces are bridged</li> <li><strong>Troubleshooting surface</strong> when something does not deliver</li> <li><strong>Knowledge required</strong> of operators who now need to understand a third networking model</li> </ul> <p><em>Use Reticulum when transport independence solves a requirement you genuinely have, not because it supports more interface types than the alternative.</em> A single LoRa mesh with a hop-limit problem is a Meshtastic or MeshCore tuning problem. It is not a transport-independence problem, and Reticulum will not make it one.</p> <hr> <h2 id="build-one-healthy-mesh-before-you-build-three-fragmented-ones"> <a href="#build-one-healthy-mesh-before-you-build-three-fragmented-ones" title="Build One Healthy Mesh Before You Build Three Fragmented Ones">Build One Healthy Mesh Before You Build Three Fragmented Ones</a> <a href="#build-one-healthy-mesh-before-you-build-three-fragmented-ones" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Build One Healthy Mesh Before You Build Three Fragmented Ones">#</a> </h2> <p>If one protocol already meets your requirements, <strong>build one healthy network</strong> instead of several smaller networks stitched together through bridges. This is the “one mesh first” principle, and it should govern most of the decisions above.</p> <p>For a community network, <strong>interoperability among the people already using it usually matters more than architectural flexibility.</strong> A large, functioning single-protocol network holds more practical value than three technically interesting but fragmented ones only partially talking to each other.</p> <h3 id="existing-meshtastic-networks-matter"> <a href="#existing-meshtastic-networks-matter" title="Existing Meshtastic Networks Matter">Existing Meshtastic Networks Matter</a> <a href="#existing-meshtastic-networks-matter" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Existing Meshtastic Networks Matter">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Do not dismiss Meshtastic simply because MeshCore has architectural advantages for fixed infrastructure.</strong> If a city already has dozens or hundreds of Meshtastic nodes, this installed base represents real infrastructure and a real community, and migration carries a cost a spec-sheet comparison fails to capture:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Installed hardware</strong> needing reflashing or replacement</li> <li><strong>Existing users</strong> already knowing how to operate the network</li> <li><strong>Community knowledge</strong> built up around the existing deployment</li> <li><strong>Repeaters already deployed</strong> and sited, sometimes on hard-won rooftop or tower access</li> <li><strong>Configuration experience</strong> accumulated by whoever runs the network</li> <li><strong>Established channels</strong> people already monitor</li> <li><strong>Training requirements</strong> for anyone learning a second system</li> </ul> <p>Protocol selection here is <strong>partly an engineering problem and partly a community adoption problem.</strong> The better architecture on paper does not automatically win if it means asking an existing, working community to start over.</p> <hr> <h2 id="the-regional-network-problem"> <a href="#the-regional-network-problem" title="The Regional-Network Problem">The Regional-Network Problem</a> <a href="#the-regional-network-problem" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Regional-Network Problem">#</a> </h2> <p>Consider a hypothetical multi-city deployment:</p> <p><strong>City A, repeater, repeater, rural relay, repeater, City B, repeater, City C</strong></p> <p>Ask how each architecture handles this as it grows. A flooding-based mesh with a hop limit of 7 struggles to span this kind of chain reliably, since every hop compounds airtime cost and every additional active node along the way adds contention. A structured, repeater-based architecture like MeshCore’s is built for exactly this shape: known relay points, deliberate placement, and routing scaling with active conversations rather than total node count.</p> <p>This is the scenario where <strong>hop limits, airtime budget, routing behavior, and infrastructure design stop being theoretical</strong> and start determining whether the network works end to end. Geographic scale is where the architectural differences between Meshtastic and MeshCore stop being academic.</p> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org/", "@type": "ImageObject", "contentUrl": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "caption": "Diagram of a regional mesh network chain linking three cities through a series of repeaters and a rural relay, illustrating how airtime and hop count compound over distance", "license": "https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/", "acquireLicensePage": "https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/", "creditText": "SimeonOnSecurity", "creator": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity" }, "copyrightNotice": "SimeonOnSecurity", "associatedArticle": { "@type": "NewsArticle", "headline": "simeononsecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/", "datePublished": "2026-09-12 23:23:19.883950818 \u002b0000 UTC m=\u002b511.610355297", "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "SimeonOnSecurity", "url": "https:\/\/simeononsecurity.ch\/authors\/simeononsecurity" } } } </script> <center> <figure align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto;" itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/ImageObject"> <meta property="article:published_time" content="2026-09-12 23:23:19.883950818 +0000 UTC m=+511.610355297"> <meta property="article:author" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <meta property="article:author:url" content="https://simeononsecurity.ch/authors/simeononsecurity"> <meta property="og:license" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/termsandconditions/"> <meta property="og:see_also" content="https://simeononsecurity.com/contactus/"> <meta property="og:copyright" content="SimeonOnSecurity"> <img align="center" style="text-align: center; margin: 0 auto; max-width: 80%; max-height: 600px; min-width: 100px; min-height: 100px; height: auto; width: auto;" src="https://simeononsecurity.ch/regional-mesh-network-repeater-chain-scaling.webp" alt="Diagram of a regional mesh network chain linking three cities through a series of repeaters and a rural relay, illustrating how airtime and hop count compound over distance"loading="lazy" fetchpriority="low" itemprop="contentUrl" /> </figure> </center> <hr> <h2 id="rf-still-matters-more-than-protocol"> <a href="#rf-still-matters-more-than-protocol" title="RF Still Matters More Than Protocol">RF Still Matters More Than Protocol</a> <a href="#rf-still-matters-more-than-protocol" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="RF Still Matters More Than Protocol">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>No amount of clever routing software creates an RF path where none physically exists.</strong> Before blaming a protocol for a coverage problem, check the fundamentals:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Antenna height</strong> above obstructions</li> <li><strong>Line of sight</strong> between the two ends of a link</li> <li><strong>Fresnel zone clearance</strong>, distinct from visual line of sight</li> <li><strong>Feed-line losses</strong> from cheap or overly long coax</li> <li><strong>Antenna quality</strong> and whether it matches the band in use</li> <li><strong>Noise floor</strong> at the receiving site</li> <li><strong>Terrain</strong> between nodes</li> <li><strong>Node placement</strong>, including the realistic room for improvement</li> <li><strong>Link margin</strong>, the buffer between signal received and the minimum needed to decode</li> </ul> <p><em>A well-positioned 2 dBi antenna on a good mast often outperforms a poorly positioned high-gain antenna in a basement window.</em> Protocol choice determines how the network handles the links you have. It does not create links where the physics will not support them.</p> <h3 id="reliability-over-maximum-range"> <a href="#reliability-over-maximum-range" title="Reliability Over Maximum Range">Reliability Over Maximum Range</a> <a href="#reliability-over-maximum-range" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reliability Over Maximum Range">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Do not design a network around the absolute edge of what a link occasionally achieves.</strong> Design around links working consistently.</p> <p>For a community or emergency-communications network, <strong>predictable delivery at 15 miles carries more practical value than a link occasionally completing at 40 miles and failing the rest of the time.</strong> Build overlapping coverage with reliable infrastructure rather than chasing record-setting single links. This principle holds regardless of which protocol carries the traffic.</p> <hr> <h2 id="which-one-to-choose"> <a href="#which-one-to-choose" title="Which One to Choose">Which One to Choose</a> <a href="#which-one-to-choose" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Which One to Choose">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Meshtastic makes sense</strong> when you value ecosystem maturity, ease of adoption, portable and roaming users, and compatibility with an existing Meshtastic community. It is the right default for most people starting from nothing.</p> <p><strong>MeshCore becomes compelling</strong> when you are intentionally building persistent LoRa infrastructure and want dedicated repeaters to form a larger, structured network. It rewards planning and rewards good repeater placement more directly than a flooding-based design does.</p> <p><strong>Reticulum makes sense</strong> when the problem extends beyond one LoRa mesh, and you need to connect different transports or otherwise separate networks into a single addressable system.</p> <p>For a <strong>license-free, low-power, long-range community infrastructure network built primarily around fixed repeaters</strong>, lean toward MeshCore. <em>If a healthy Meshtastic network already exists in your area, replacing it needs enough benefit to justify fragmenting the existing community.</em> Reticulum enters the picture when one mesh protocol, or one physical transport, no longer meets the requirement, not simply because it does more things.</p> <hr> <h2 id="references"> <a href="#references" title="References">References</a> <a href="#references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="References">#</a> </h2> <ol> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MeshCore Official Site"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://meshcore.co.uk/"> <a href="https://meshcore.co.uk/" rel="noopener rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Reticulum Configuring Interfaces</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MeshCore vs Meshtastic Comparison Guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/meshcore-vs-meshtastic-comparison-guide/"> <a href="/articles/meshcore-vs-meshtastic-comparison-guide/" rel="follow me" >MeshCore vs Meshtastic Comparison Guide</a> </span> </li> </ol> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: HackTheBox - Sherlock - PhantomRing
item.category: "HackTheBox" , "Sherlock" , "DFIR" , "Malware Analysis" , "Static Analysis" , "ELF" , "objdump" , "strings" , "nm" , "sha256sum" , "EDR evasion" , "eBPF" , "SUID" , "CTF" , "Linux malware" , "reverse engineering"
item.description: A walkthrough of the PhantomRing Sherlock on HackTheBox: statically analyzing a Linux ELF agent with file, nm, strings, and objdump to pull the C2 details, privesc checks, and self-destruct logic without ever running the binary.
item.content:encoded: <p>PhantomRing is one of the Sherlock boxes on HackTheBox, which is their forensics/malware-analysis line rather than the usual “pop a shell” Machines. You get a zip, a short scenario, and a set of questions to answer from evidence in that zip. This one hands you a single Linux binary and asks you to figure out what it does without running it, since it’s a real (if simple) piece of post-exploitation malware.</p> <hr> <h2 id="provided-files"> <a href="#provided-files" title="Provided Files:">Provided Files:</a> <a href="#provided-files" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Provided Files:">#</a> </h2> <p>You get <code>phantomring.zip</code>, password protected (HTB gives you the password on the download page), containing one file:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code>phantom_ring/agent </code></pre><p>The scenario is basically: a SOC team found this binary sitting in <code>/var/tmp</code> on a box, it was making outbound connections, and you need to work out what it’s capable of and pull out IOCs, all through static analysis.</p> <h2 id="walk-through"> <a href="#walk-through" title="Walk Through:">Walk Through:</a> <a href="#walk-through" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Walk Through:">#</a> </h2> <p>First thing, don’t run it. It’s live malware, so everything below is read-only inspection.</p> <h3 id="basic-triage"> <a href="#basic-triage" title="Basic triage">Basic triage</a> <a href="#basic-triage" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Basic triage">#</a> </h3> <p>Once extracted, start with the boring stuff:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>file phantom_ring/agent </span></span></code></pre></div><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>phantom_ring/agent: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, version 1 (SYSV), </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>BuildID[sha1]=<build id>, </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>for GNU/Linux 3.2.0, not stripped </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Not stripped is the important bit here. That means the symbol table is still in the binary, so function names survive. Grab the hash while you’re at it since it’s usually one of the scored questions on these:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>sha256sum phantom_ring/agent </span></span></code></pre></div><h3 id="looking-at-the-symbols-before-touching-the-disassembler"> <a href="#looking-at-the-symbols-before-touching-the-disassembler" title="Looking at the symbols before touching the disassembler">Looking at the symbols before touching the disassembler</a> <a href="#looking-at-the-symbols-before-touching-the-disassembler" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Looking at the symbols before touching the disassembler">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>nm phantom_ring/agent | grep <span style="color:#e6db74">' T \| t '</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>This lists every function name in the binary. Because it wasn’t stripped, you get real names instead of <code>sub_401230</code>-style garbage. Scanning through, a few things stand out immediately:</p> <ul> <li>A block of local helper symbols that all share one distinctive name prefix (things like <code><prefix>_prep_read</code>, <code><prefix>_wait_cqe</code>, <code><prefix>_cq_advance</code>), plus a couple of higher-level wrapper functions (a file reader, <code>send_all</code>, <code>recv_all</code>) built on top of them. That shared prefix names a specific Linux async I/O kernel interface, and every one of the agent’s own file and socket operations routes through it instead of libc’s classic <code>read</code>/<code>write</code>/<code>connect</code>/<code>open</code> wrappers. That’s the answer to “which kernel interface does it abuse for EDR evasion”, you just need to recognize the prefix and know why malware likes hiding behind that particular interface.</li> <li>A run of <code>cmd_*</code> functions (things like <code>cmd_get</code>, <code>cmd_recv</code>, <code>cmd_privesc</code>, <code>cmd_selfdestruct</code>, and several more in the same style), plus <code>process_cmd</code> and <code>main</code>. That’s the command handler layout right there, one function per capability, and the exact count is worth writing down for later.</li> </ul> <p>Worth flagging early: the number of <code>cmd_*</code> handler symbols here is not automatically the same as the number of distinct commands the dispatcher exposes to a connected client. That distinction matters later.</p> <p>I used this list as a map for the rest of the analysis, jumping straight to whichever <code>cmd_*</code> function was relevant instead of reading the whole disassembly top to bottom.</p> <h3 id="pulling-strings"> <a href="#pulling-strings" title="Pulling strings">Pulling strings</a> <a href="#pulling-strings" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Pulling strings">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>strings -n <span style="color:#ae81ff">4</span> phantom_ring/agent </span></span></code></pre></div><p>This is always worth doing early since it’s free and this binary didn’t bother hiding anything. Scrolling through the output you get a good chunk of the picture right away:</p> <ul> <li>A procfs-style path right next to <code>"Logged users:"</code> and its matching <code>"Error reading ..."</code> message. That’s the login-enumeration file <code>cmd_users</code> parses, a classic session-tracking table.</li> <li><code>/proc</code>, <code>/proc/%ld/comm</code>, <code>/proc/%ld/fd</code>, <code>/dev/pts</code> sitting near a <code>"PID CMD"</code> header, which is <code>cmd_ps</code> walking procfs to list processes.</li> <li>A single directory path grouped with <code>"Failed to open ..."</code> and <code>"Potential SUID binaries:"</code>. That’s the SUID scan directory in <code>cmd_privesc</code>, no ambiguity about which string it is, just not naming it here.</li> <li><code>"Agent will self-destruct"</code> and <code>"Unlink failed: %s"</code> bracketing a procfs path in <code>cmd_selfdestruct</code>. That path is what it reads to find its own location on disk before deleting itself.</li> <li>Three <code>/sys/kernel/debug/tracing/...</code> paths back to back, plus <code>"[*] Tracing disabled: %s"</code>. Three candidates for “first tracing file disabled”, but <code>strings</code> just dumps them in file order, it doesn’t tell you which one the code actually touches first.</li> <li><code>/sys/fs/bpf</code>, a <code>/proc/%s/maps</code>-style format string, a short marker string, and <code>"[+] Killed PID using BPF: %d"</code> clustered together, which is the eBPF/killbpf detection logic. The format string is what it builds per PID, the marker is the substring it hunts for inside that file. What <code>strings</code> alone doesn’t tell you is <em>when</em> in the loop that check runs relative to the tracing-file cleanup in the same handler.</li> <li>A short run of two-to-eight character tokens right before the <code>"[*] 404 Command not found [*]"</code> message: these are the literal command names the dispatcher compares against, one of which triggers self-destruction.</li> <li>One dotted-quad IPv4 address sitting completely alone in the string table, right next to the literal <code>socket</code> symbol name and one of the async-I/O helper symbols mentioned above. That’s the hardcoded C2 address, in the clear, no obfuscation attempted.</li> <li><code>"connect() failed: trying to reconnect"</code> and <code>"[+] Connected to %s:%d"</code> bracketing the connect logic.</li> </ul> <p><em>What <code>strings</code> cannot give you</em>: the port number, the reconnect delay, which of the three tracing paths is disabled first, which of the two procfs paths feeds the eBPF <code>strstr</code> check, and the true count of distinct commands. All five of those live only as numeric operands or control-flow order in the machine code, never as printable text. For those you have to read the disassembly.</p> <h3 id="digging-into-the-disassembly"> <a href="#digging-into-the-disassembly" title="Digging into the disassembly">Digging into the disassembly</a> <a href="#digging-into-the-disassembly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Digging into the disassembly">#</a> </h3> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn phantom_ring/agent > disasm.txt </span></span></code></pre></div><p>First annoyance: this binary was built with the hardened PLT (<code>.plt.sec</code>), so <code>objdump</code> prints calls to it as a bare offset like <code>callq 0x12c0 <.plt.sec+0x10></code> instead of a friendly name. Before reading anything else I resolved that table once so every later call site would be self-explanatory. <code>.plt.sec</code> is a block of 16-byte stubs starting at <code>0x12b0</code>, each one doing <code>endbr64</code> then <code>jmpq *offset(%rip)</code> into a GOT slot, and <code>objdump -R</code> prints exactly which imported symbol lives in each GOT slot:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>objdump -R phantom_ring/agent </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Lining up GOT addresses against stub addresses (stub base = GOT-slot-relative jump target minus 4 bytes for the <code>endbr64</code>) gives a lookup table, for example <code>.plt.sec+0x10</code> is <code>strncmp</code>, <code>+0x70</code> is <code>strlen</code>, <code>+0x1c0</code> is <code>readdir</code>… once you have that table written down, every <code>callq 0x12xx <.plt.sec+...></code> in the rest of the disassembly reads like a normal function call.</p> <p><strong>Port and reconnect delay.</strong> Inside <code>main()</code>, right before the connect sequence, there’s this:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>41f7: movw $0x2, -0x10100(%rbp) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>4200: movl $<port immediate>, %edi </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>4205: callq 0x1350 <.plt.sec+0xa0> ; htons </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>420a: movw %ax, -0x100fe(%rbp) </span></span></code></pre></div><p><code>0x1350</code> resolves to <code>htons</code> in the PLT table. It’s called with a 16-bit immediate loaded straight into <code>%edi</code>, and the byte-swapped result gets written into the port field of the sockaddr struct sitting on the stack. That immediate, converted from hex to decimal, is the C2 port, and it’s a literal instruction operand, no guessing or dynamic computation involved.</p> <p>Further down, on the failed-connect path right after the <code>"connect() failed: trying to reconnect"</code> string reference, there’s a <code>movl $<delay immediate>, %edi</code> immediately followed by a call into <code>.plt.sec+0x230</code>, which the PLT table resolves to <code>sleep</code>. That immediate, converted to decimal, is the reconnect back-off delay in seconds.</p> <p><strong>Command dispatch and the real count.</strong> <code>process_cmd</code> is a straight chain of length-checked <code>strncmp</code>/<code>strcmp</code> calls, each one comparing the sanitized input against one literal token before branching to a handler:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>3ebf: leaq <offset>(%rip), %rcx ; -> literal command token </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>3ecc: callq 0x12c0 <.plt.sec+0x10> ; strncmp </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>3ed3: testl %eax, %eax </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>3ed5: jne <next comparison> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>... </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>3ee9: callq 0x23da <cmd_get> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>That pattern repeats once per candidate command, and every branch target is one of the <code>cmd_*</code> symbols from the <code>nm</code> output. Walking the whole chain and writing down (literal string, target handler) for each comparison is the only reliable way to build a full command inventory, and it’s what exposes the twist: one pair of literal tokens, a short one and a longer alias of it, both branch to the <em>exact same</em> <code>callq</code> target address. <code>strings</code> alone would never show you that, since it just lists both tokens as separate text with no idea they resolve to one implementation. The real “how many distinct commands” answer is the count of unique handler addresses actually called from this chain, not the count of literal strings sitting in <code>.rodata</code>, and those two counts are not equal here.</p> <p><strong>SUID scan and eBPF/tracing evasion.</strong> <code>cmd_privesc</code> calls one of the async-I/O prep helpers to stat a path, then <code>opendir</code> (<code>.plt.sec+0x1c0</code>) against a single hardcoded path loaded via <code>leaq</code> right before the call, no loop, no user input, one fixed directory.
