item.category: "IT homelab 2026" , "building an IT home lab" , "homelab career" , "IT portfolio homelab" , "Proxmox homelab" , "homelab for job seekers" , "IT lab setup" , "homelab documentation career" , "homelab github" , "IT career proof of work"
item.description: In 2026, a well-documented IT homelab is the most important thing you can build for your career. Certifications are checkboxes. Your homelab proves you can actually do the work.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook"> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook" title=" Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook</a> </span> </a> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>A well-run and documented homelab is the single most important thing you can build for your IT career in 2026.</strong> Not a certification. Not a degree. Not a LinkedIn endorsement. A real, running, documented environment that proves you have deployed systems, broken them, fixed them, automated them, and learned from every incident. <em>In the age of AI-generated resumes and credential inflation, the homelab is the one thing that cannot be faked.</em></p> <h2 id="why-the-homelab-matters-more-than-ever-in-2026"> <a href="#why-the-homelab-matters-more-than-ever-in-2026" title="Why the Homelab Matters More Than Ever in 2026">Why the Homelab Matters More Than Ever in 2026</a> <a href="#why-the-homelab-matters-more-than-ever-in-2026" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why the Homelab Matters More Than Ever in 2026">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>AI has changed what “qualified” looks like.</strong> Generative AI can write a compelling resume for anyone. AI tutoring tools can help someone pass a CompTIA exam without ever touching real hardware. Hiring managers have seen the result: a flood of applicants who can describe how a thing works but cannot troubleshoot it when it breaks on a live system.</p> <p>The homelab cuts through this directly. When you sit in an interview and describe:</p> <ul> <li>“My Proxmox cluster had a storage pool corruption event after a failed ZFS scrub. Here is how I diagnosed it, restored from backup, and wrote the postmortem.”</li> <li>“I automated 90% of my user provisioning with Ansible and Vault. Here is the repo.”</li> <li>“I ran a Wazuh SIEM with custom detection rules and documented three false positive tuning cycles.”</li> </ul> <p>…that is something no AI wrote for you. Interviewers know this. The homelab is your proof of work.</p> <h2 id="the-mindset-shift-homelab-as-continuous-practice"> <a href="#the-mindset-shift-homelab-as-continuous-practice" title="The Mindset Shift: Homelab as Continuous Practice">The Mindset Shift: Homelab as Continuous Practice</a> <a href="#the-mindset-shift-homelab-as-continuous-practice" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Mindset Shift: Homelab as Continuous Practice">#</a> </h2> <p>Do not build a homelab once for a certification and abandon it. That is the wrong mental model. Think of the homelab as your permanent professional practice environment — something you add to, break, rebuild, document, and evolve continuously throughout your career.</p> <p>The best homelabs in 2026 look like this:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Always running</strong>: services are live, monitored, and alerting.</li> <li><strong>Continuously documented</strong>: every major change is documented with a runbook or incident report.</li> <li><strong>Version controlled</strong>: infrastructure configurations and scripts live in a git repo.</li> <li><strong>Publicly referenced</strong>: your GitHub or portfolio site links to the documentation and architecture diagrams.</li> <li><strong>Deliberately broken and fixed</strong>: you intentionally introduce failures to practice incident response.</li> </ul> <h2 id="what-to-build-by-career-target"> <a href="#what-to-build-by-career-target" title="What to Build (By Career Target)">What to Build (By Career Target)</a> <a href="#what-to-build-by-career-target" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What to Build (By Career Target)">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="it-support--sysadmin-track"> <a href="#it-support--sysadmin-track" title="IT Support / Sysadmin Track">IT Support / Sysadmin Track</a> <a href="#it-support--sysadmin-track" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="IT Support / Sysadmin Track">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>What to Build</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Hypervisor</strong></td> <td>Proxmox VE cluster (2–3 nodes)</td> <td>Multi-node experience is what production looks like</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Active Directory</strong></td> <td>Windows Server 2022 domain with GPOs, OU structure, group policies</td> <td>AD is in every enterprise; know it cold</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Linux servers</strong></td> <td>Ubuntu and Rocky Linux VMs running real services (Nginx, Samba, SSH hardened)</td> <td>Linux is in everything</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Monitoring</strong></td> <td>Zabbix or Grafana + Prometheus stack monitoring all VMs</td> <td>Observability is a required skill</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Backup</strong></td> <td>Veeam or Proxmox Backup Server with tested restore procedures</td> <td>Untested backups are not backups</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Ticketing</strong></td> <td>Freshdesk or osTicket running on a VM</td> <td>Practice the workflow you will live in at work</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Network</strong></td> <td>VLANs, pfSense or OPNsense firewall, managed switch, IDS</td> <td>Real network segmentation and traffic analysis</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="cloud--devops-track"> <a href="#cloud--devops-track" title="Cloud / DevOps Track">Cloud / DevOps Track</a> <a href="#cloud--devops-track" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Cloud / DevOps Track">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>What to Build</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>IaC</strong></td> <td>Terraform-managed AWS or Azure resources in a free-tier account</td> <td>IaC is now baseline; not knowing it is a red flag</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>CI/CD</strong></td> <td>GitHub Actions or GitLab CI pipeline for at least one deployed service</td> <td>Automated pipelines are table stakes</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Containers</strong></td> <td>Docker Compose lab progressing to k3s or K8s</td> <td>Container orchestration is required at most cloud shops</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Monitoring</strong></td> <td>Datadog free tier or self-hosted Prometheus/Grafana</td> <td>Ship nothing you cannot observe</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Secrets management</strong></td> <td>HashiCorp Vault</td> <td>Hardcoded credentials in your repos will end interviews</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h3 id="security-track"> <a href="#security-track" title="Security Track">Security Track</a> <a href="#security-track" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Security Track">#</a> </h3> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Component</th> <th>What to Build</th> <th>Why It Matters</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>SIEM</strong></td> <td>Wazuh or Security Onion collecting from all homelab assets</td> <td>Alert fatigue and tuning is the real job</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Vulnerability scanning</strong></td> <td>OpenVAS or Tenable Nessus Essentials</td> <td>Run regular scans, document and remediate findings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Attack lab</strong></td> <td>Isolated VLAN with Metasploitable and DVWA for practice attacks</td> <td>Offensive awareness makes better defenders</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Firewall/IDS</strong></td> <td>Suricata on OPNsense with custom rules</td> <td>Rule writing is a differentiating skill</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Threat intel</strong></td> <td>MISP or OpenCTI consuming public threat feeds</td> <td>Threat intel integration is a senior skill most juniors lack</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="the-documentation-system-that-gets-you-hired"> <a href="#the-documentation-system-that-gets-you-hired" title="The Documentation System That Gets You Hired">The Documentation System That Gets You Hired</a> <a href="#the-documentation-system-that-gets-you-hired" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Documentation System That Gets You Hired">#</a> </h2> <p>Your homelab’s documentation is as important as the lab itself. A common mistake: building a complex environment but leaving nothing written down. The documentation is what you share in interviews, reference on your resume, and post publicly to build credibility.</p> <p>Structure your documentation to include:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Architecture diagram</strong> — a network/system diagram showing every component, VLAN, and connection. Use draw.io or Excalidraw, export as PNG, commit to GitHub.</li> <li><strong>Service inventory</strong> — a table of every running service, its purpose, its host, and its current status.</li> <li><strong>Runbooks</strong> — step-by-step procedures for common tasks (backup restoration, password reset, certificate renewal, adding a new VM).</li> <li><strong>Incident reports</strong> — for every major failure or misconfiguration, write a short postmortem: what happened, what you did, what you learned, and what you changed.</li> <li><strong>Change log</strong> — a running log of major changes to the environment with dates and rationale.</li> </ol> <p><strong>Put all of this in a public GitHub repository.</strong> Link it from your resume and LinkedIn profile. This is your portfolio.</p> <h2 id="hardware-to-start-with"> <a href="#hardware-to-start-with" title="Hardware to Start With">Hardware to Start With</a> <a href="#hardware-to-start-with" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hardware to Start With">#</a> </h2> <p>You do not need expensive hardware to build a useful homelab. A realistic minimum:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Option</th> <th>Cost</th> <th>What You Get</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>One used Dell/HP SFF workstation</strong></td> <td>$100–$200</td> <td>16–32GB RAM, enough for 5–8 VMs, Proxmox single node</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Two SFF workstations</strong></td> <td>$200–$400</td> <td>Mini Proxmox cluster with live migration practice</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Used enterprise server (R730/R720)</strong></td> <td>$150–$400</td> <td>Full ECC RAM, RAID, IPMI — real datacenter experience</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Raspberry Pi cluster</strong></td> <td>$150–$300</td> <td>ARM-based Kubernetes lab, low power</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Managed switch</strong></td> <td>$30–$80 used</td> <td>VLAN practice, trunk ports, STP, real switching experience</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Cloud free tiers (AWS, Azure, GCP) supplement physical hardware. Use AWS Free Tier for anything requiring cloud-specific services. Keep the physical homelab for network, AD, and storage work.</p> <h2 id="what-to-avoid"> <a href="#what-to-avoid" title="What to Avoid">What to Avoid</a> <a href="#what-to-avoid" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="What to Avoid">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Never put untested backups in a runbook.</strong> Test every restore procedure before writing it down. A runbook that says “restore from backup” when the backup has not been verified is a liability.</li> <li><strong>Do not run services on your ISP’s network exposed to the internet</strong> without a reverse proxy, proper firewall rules, and fail2ban or equivalent. Security practice starts in your own lab.</li> <li><strong>Do not document only the happy path.</strong> Interviewers are interested in the failures and recoveries. Document incidents honestly.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Is IT a Good Career?"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/is-it-a-good-career/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/is-it-a-good-career/" rel="follow me" >Is IT a Good Career?</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT Training Resources Online"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/it-training-resources-online/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/getting-started-in-it/it-training-resources-online/" rel="follow me" >IT Training Resources Online</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT Career Playbook Home"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >IT Career Playbook Home</a> </span> </li> </ul> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Building and Leading a Development Team
item.category: "building a development team" , "leading a software engineering team" , "engineering manager 1:1s" , "hiring software developers" , "code review culture" , "software team culture" , "team health metrics" , "managing a development team"
item.description: How to build and lead a high-performing software development team — hiring for technical and cultural fit, running effective 1:1s, building code review culture, and sustaining team health.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="click-here-to-return-to-the-software-development-career-playbook"> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-software-development-career-playbook" title=" Click Here to Return To the Software Development Career Playbook "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the Software Development Career Playbook"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/software-development-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/software-development-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the Software Development Career Playbook</a> </span> </a> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-software-development-career-playbook" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" Click Here to Return To the Software Development Career Playbook ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>A software engineering team’s output is not the sum of its individuals’ capabilities. It is the product of how well those individuals collaborate, communicate, and support each other.</strong> A team of strong junior engineers with excellent culture and clear ownership will consistently outperform a team of exceptional engineers with unclear roles and poor communication. <em>The engineering manager’s job is to build and sustain the conditions under which engineers can do their best work.</em></p> <h2 id="hiring-for-your-team"> <a href="#hiring-for-your-team" title="Hiring for Your Team">Hiring for Your Team</a> <a href="#hiring-for-your-team" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Hiring for Your Team">#</a> </h2> <p>Every hire either raises or lowers the average. Define what you need concretely before opening a requisition.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Write the job description around outcomes, not requirements.</strong> “Owns the reliability and performance of our payments API” is more honest and attracts better candidates than “7+ years of experience with Python.”</li> <li><strong>Define your evaluation rubric before you start interviews.</strong> What does a strong answer look like for each question? Do not calibrate after you have met candidates.</li> <li><strong>Structure your interview process</strong>: recruiter screen, technical assessment, behavioral round, team fit conversation. Do not invent the format as you go.</li> <li><strong>Diversify your sourcing</strong>: referrals, targeted outreach on LinkedIn, bootcamp placement partnerships, open source community presence. Relying solely on inbound applications limits your candidate pool.</li> </ul> <h2 id="technical-interview-design"> <a href="#technical-interview-design" title="Technical Interview Design">Technical Interview Design</a> <a href="#technical-interview-design" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Technical Interview Design">#</a> </h2> <p>Avoid trivia and gotcha questions. They measure recall, not engineering ability. Effective technical interviews:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Format</th> <th>What It Measures</th> <th>Notes</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>System design discussion</strong></td> <td>Architecture reasoning, trade-off awareness</td> <td>Best for mid to senior hires</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Live coding with context</strong></td> <td>Problem-solving process, communication, code quality</td> <td>Give the problem in advance; evaluate approach not speed</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Take-home project</strong></td> <td>Code quality, documentation, judgment</td> <td>Keep scope to 2 to 3 hours maximum</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Code review exercise</strong></td> <td>Code reading, feedback quality, communication</td> <td>Underused but excellent signal for collaborative fit</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Past project walkthrough</strong></td> <td>Depth of ownership, technical judgment in real projects</td> <td>Behavioral + technical combined</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="running-effective-11-meetings"> <a href="#running-effective-11-meetings" title="Running Effective 1:1 Meetings">Running Effective 1:1 Meetings</a> <a href="#running-effective-11-meetings" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Running Effective 1:1 Meetings">#</a> </h2> <p>A 1:1 is your most important management tool. Every direct report deserves a weekly or bi-weekly private conversation.</p> <p><strong>What a good 1:1 is:</strong></p> <ul> <li>A conversation driven primarily by the engineer’s agenda, not yours.</li> <li>A space to surface problems, concerns, and ambitions that would not come up in group settings.</li> <li>A relationship-building investment that compounds over time.</li> </ul> <p><strong>What a good 1:1 is not:</strong></p> <ul> <li>A status update meeting (that belongs in stand-up or async tools).</li> <li>A place to deliver performance feedback for the first time (feedback should be continuous, not saved).</li> </ul> <p>A basic 1:1 format that works:</p> <ol> <li>“What is on your mind?” — open-ended start.</li> <li>Discuss any ongoing career development themes.</li> <li>Address any blocking or context they need from you.</li> <li>End with one clear action item (ideally theirs, not just yours).</li> </ol> <h2 id="building-a-healthy-code-review-culture"> <a href="#building-a-healthy-code-review-culture" title="Building a Healthy Code Review Culture">Building a Healthy Code Review Culture</a> <a href="#building-a-healthy-code-review-culture" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Building a Healthy Code Review Culture">#</a> </h2> <p>Code review is the primary on-the-job learning mechanism for most engineers. Culture around it matters.</p> <p><strong>Signs of a healthy code review culture:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Reviews happen within 24 hours of submission.</li> <li>Comments explain the reasoning behind suggestions, not just flag problems.</li> <li>Positive feedback is given as readily as corrective feedback.</li> <li>Major architectural disagreements are resolved in design discussions before code is written.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Signs of an unhealthy code review culture:</strong></p> <ul> <li>Reviews are used to assert dominance rather than improve quality.</li> <li>PRs sit unreviewed for days or weeks.</li> <li>Engineers stop asking questions for fear of being judged.</li> <li>Reviews become rubber stamps out of exhaustion.</li> </ul> <h2 id="sustaining-team-health"> <a href="#sustaining-team-health" title="Sustaining Team Health">Sustaining Team Health</a> <a href="#sustaining-team-health" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Sustaining Team Health">#</a> </h2> <p>Team health is measurable. Three lightweight signals to track:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Velocity</strong>: is the team shipping consistently? Erratic velocity signals unclear priorities, excessive meetings, or morale issues.</li> <li><strong>Retention</strong>: are engineers leaving at above-normal rates? Exit interview themes reveal systemic issues.</li> <li><strong>Psychological safety</strong>: do engineers raise risks and ask for help, or do problems surface only when they become crises?</li> </ul> <p>Quarterly retrospectives give the team a structured channel to surface problems. Act on retrospective feedback visibly. Teams that raise problems and see them ignored stop raising problems.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Engineering Management Career Path"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/software-development-career-playbook/managing-a-development-team/engineering-management-career-path/"> <a href="/software-development-career-playbook/managing-a-development-team/engineering-management-career-path/" rel="follow me" >Engineering Management Career Path</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Software Development Methodologies"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/software-development-career-playbook/managing-a-development-team/software-development-methodologies-agile-scrum-kanban/"> <a href="/software-development-career-playbook/managing-a-development-team/software-development-methodologies-agile-scrum-kanban/" rel="follow me" >Software Development Methodologies</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Software Development Career Playbook Home"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/software-development-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/software-development-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >Software Development Career Playbook Home</a> </span> </li> </ul> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/

item.title: Building and Managing an IT Team
item.category: "building an it team" , "it team management" , "it hiring guide" , "it onboarding" , "it team structure" , "managing it staff" , "it manager tips" , "managing an it team" , "it career playbook"
item.description: Learn how to build and manage a high-performing IT team, from defining team structure and writing job descriptions to running effective onboarding and retaining talent.
item.content:encoded: <h4 id="click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook"> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook" title=" Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook "> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook</a> </span> </a> <a href="#click-here-to-return-to-the-it-career-playbook" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title=" Click Here to Return To the IT Career Playbook ">#</a> </h4> <p><strong>Building a great IT team is the highest-leverage thing an IT manager can do.</strong> A well-structured team with clear ownership and strong onboarding multiplies your department’s output and resilience. <em>One strong hire compounds over years. One bad hire costs months of management time and damages team morale.</em></p> <p>The structure, hiring process, and onboarding program you build define what your team can accomplish long after any individual contributor’s contributions fade.</p> <h2 id="designing-your-team-structure"> <a href="#designing-your-team-structure" title="Designing Your Team Structure">Designing Your Team Structure</a> <a href="#designing-your-team-structure" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Designing Your Team Structure">#</a> </h2> <p>Before hiring, define what the team needs to accomplish and map roles to functions. Common IT team structures:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Model</th> <th>Best For</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Functional silos</strong> (network, security, helpdesk)</td> <td>Larger orgs with specialized workloads</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Generalist pods</strong></td> <td>Small orgs where everyone shares ownership</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Product-aligned squads</strong></td> <td>Companies with multiple internal platforms</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Tiered support</strong> (L1/L2/L3)</td> <td>Service desk and managed service environments</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Document the responsibilities of each role before you open a requisition. Vague job descriptions attract mismatched candidates and create role-conflict problems after hire.</p> <h2 id="writing-effective-job-descriptions"> <a href="#writing-effective-job-descriptions" title="Writing Effective Job Descriptions">Writing Effective Job Descriptions</a> <a href="#writing-effective-job-descriptions" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Writing Effective Job Descriptions">#</a> </h2> <p>A good IT job description is specific enough to self-select the right candidates and honest about the environment. Include:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Required skills</strong>: be realistic. List only what is genuinely required, not a wish list.</li> <li><strong>Day-to-day responsibilities</strong>: what will the person actually do in week one, month three, and year one?</li> <li><strong>Tools and environment</strong>: cloud provider, ticketing system, operating systems, team size.</li> <li><strong>Growth potential</strong>: where does this role lead? Candidates evaluate trajectory.</li> </ul> <p>Avoid listing 12 required certifications for a role that needs two. Inflated requirements reduce applicant quality by filtering out strong generalists.</p> <h2 id="interviewing-for-it-roles"> <a href="#interviewing-for-it-roles" title="Interviewing for IT Roles">Interviewing for IT Roles</a> <a href="#interviewing-for-it-roles" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interviewing for IT Roles">#</a> </h2> <p>Structure your interview process to evaluate technical skill, communication, and culture fit separately. A useful three-stage process:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Recruiter screen</strong> — confirms baseline qualifications, comp expectations, and availability.</li> <li><strong>Technical assessment</strong> — scenario-based questions, a take-home task, or a live troubleshooting exercise. Avoid trivia. Evaluate problem-solving process, not memorized answers.</li> <li><strong>Panel interview</strong> — a senior technical peer and one stakeholder assess communication, collaboration, and judgment.</li> </ol> <p><em>Document evaluation criteria before interviews begin so all candidates are scored consistently and your decision survives a legal challenge.</em></p> <h2 id="onboarding-that-reduces-time-to-productivity"> <a href="#onboarding-that-reduces-time-to-productivity" title="Onboarding That Reduces Time to Productivity">Onboarding That Reduces Time to Productivity</a> <a href="#onboarding-that-reduces-time-to-productivity" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Onboarding That Reduces Time to Productivity">#</a> </h2> <p>Poor onboarding wastes months of ramp-up time and signals to new hires that the organization is disorganized. Build a 30/60/90-day onboarding plan for every IT role.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Day 1</strong>: accounts provisioned, equipment ready, manager introduction, team meeting.</li> <li><strong>Week 1</strong>: shadow existing team members, review runbooks and network diagrams, read key policies.</li> <li><strong>Day 30</strong>: owns at least one recurring task or system independently.</li> <li><strong>Day 60</strong>: completing tickets and projects with minimal supervision.</li> <li><strong>Day 90</strong>: identifying process improvements and contributing to team documentation.</li> </ul> <p>Assign a dedicated onboarding buddy. New hires ask low-stakes questions of peers that they would not ask their manager.</p> <h2 id="retaining-it-talent"> <a href="#retaining-it-talent" title="Retaining IT Talent">Retaining IT Talent</a> <a href="#retaining-it-talent" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Retaining IT Talent">#</a> </h2> <p>Turnover in IT is expensive. Replacing a mid-level engineer costs 50 to 200 percent of annual salary when you factor in recruiting, ramp-up, and lost productivity. Retention levers that actually work:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Clear career path</strong>: people leave when they cannot see how to grow where they are.</li> <li><strong>Reasonable on-call burden</strong>: chronic overtime and excessive on-call rotations are the top driver of IT burnout.</li> <li><strong>Learning time</strong>: budget for certifications, conferences, and side projects. Teams that grow together stay together.</li> <li><strong>Psychological safety</strong>: a team where engineers can flag problems and propose changes without fear of blame retains talent that average teams lose.</li> </ul> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT Policies and Change Management"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/managing-an-it-team/it-policies-and-change-management/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/managing-an-it-team/it-policies-and-change-management/" rel="follow me" >IT Policies and Change Management</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Outsourcing vs. In-House IT"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook/managing-an-it-team/outsourcing-vs-inhouse-it/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook/managing-an-it-team/outsourcing-vs-inhouse-it/" rel="follow me" >Outsourcing vs. In-House IT</a> </span> </li> <li> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="IT Career Playbook Home"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/it-career-playbook-start/"> <a href="/it-career-playbook-start/" rel="follow me" >IT Career Playbook Home</a> </span> </li> </ul> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.ch/
